topics.title: The product life cycle
topics.summary: Every product moves through four stages: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. The right marketing mix changes at each stage. This topic covers how the sales and profit curves behave, the stage-by-stage management table (Figure 8-3) you must memorize, primary vs selective demand, and what to do when a product declines (deletion vs harvesting).

topics.title: PLC shapes
topics.summary: Not every product follows the textbook curve. How much a consumer must learn changes the length of the introduction stage (high-learning vs low-learning products), and fashions and fads have their own distinctive patterns. Exam questions describe a product's sales pattern and ask you to name the shape.

topics.title: Extending the PLC
topics.summary: Instead of letting a mature product slide into decline, marketers can stretch its life: modify the product, modify the market, reposition it, or introduce a new product. Know each tactic's sub-types (product improvements, line extensions, new customers, increased use, new use situations, trading up and down) and the cannibalization risk that comes with line extensions.

topics.title: Innovation, adoption and failure
topics.summary: New products are the lifeblood of a company, but they are costly and risky to develop. This topic covers how new an innovation is (minor, continuous, radical), who adopts it and when (the adoption curve and its five categories), the four barriers that stop people adopting, and the five reasons new products fail.

topics.title: Growth strategy and the NPD process
topics.summary: Firms choose where to grow using the strategic approaches to growth matrix (market penetration, product development, market development, diversification). They then follow a seven-step new product development process from strategy to commercialization. Know each step's purpose, methods and position in the sequence.

concepts.definition: The stages a new product goes through in the marketplace (introduction, growth, maturity and decline), used to help manage a product from its initial launch to its eventual decline.
concepts.explain: Think of the PLC as a product's biography. Sales (in units) rise slowly at launch, climb fast in growth, peak and plateau in maturity, and fall in decline. The profit curve lags behind sales: it is negative or minimal at introduction, reaches its maximum late in growth, levels off in maturity and then falls. The length of the cycle varies by product, and technology products tend to have much shorter cycles.
concepts.example: Smartphones moved from introduction (few buyers, high prices) through rapid growth to maturity, where Rogers, Bell and Telus now fight over subscribers with discounts and promotions.
concepts.contrast: The PLC tracks a PRODUCT's sales and profits over time; the adoption curve tracks the PEOPLE (innovators to laggards) who buy it over time. The NPD process is the seven-step internal process that happens BEFORE the PLC begins at commercialization.
concepts.trap: Watch the timing of the peaks: profits reach their maximum in GROWTH and level off in maturity, while SALES peak in maturity. A statement that 'profits peak in maturity' or 'sales peak in growth' is wrong for this course.
concepts.mnemonic: I-G-M-D: 'I Grow, Mature, Decline.' Profit peaks first (growth), sales peak second (maturity).

concepts.term: PLC stage table (Figure 8-3: managing the stages of the PLC)
concepts.definition: The course's summary of how competition, the general marketing objective, the 4 Ps (product, price, place, promotion) and profit change across the introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages.
concepts.explain: This table is a must-memorize grid: seven rows by four stages. Read each row as a story. Competitors go few, more, many, fewer. Objectives go awareness, product differentiation, brand loyalty, product rationalization. Distribution goes limited, increased, full, reduced. Most exam questions give you one or two cells and ask for the stage, or name a stage and ask for the right action.
concepts.example: A Calgary start-up launching a smart bike lock with limited distribution, awareness advertising and a skimming price is in introduction. Once rivals copy it and the company adds features and expands into more stores, it has moved to growth.
concepts.contrast: Don't mix up the objective row and the promotion row. Growth's OBJECTIVE is product differentiation and its PROMOTION emphasizes points of difference versus competitors. Maturity's objective is brand loyalty, but its promotion focuses on pricing and sales promotion.
concepts.trap: Each price cue maps to one stage: 'skimming or penetration' = introduction; 'slowly reduced' = growth; discounts 'used frequently' = maturity; 'very low prices' = decline. 'Full distribution is achieved' = maturity, NOT growth (growth = distribution is increased).
concepts.mnemonic: Objectives A-D-L-R: 'A Dog Loves Running' (Awareness, Differentiation, Loyalty, Rationalization).

concepts.definition: The first PLC stage, when a product is launched; the marketing objective is to create consumer awareness and stimulate trial, with few competitors, limited distribution and minimal profits, if any.
concepts.explain: At launch nobody knows the product, so the job is awareness and trial. Costs are high (R&D, launch advertising) and sales are low, so profits are minimal or negative. Price is set with either skimming (a high price to recover R&D) or penetration (a low price to build volume), distribution is limited, and advertising focuses on building awareness. The firm must first stimulate primary demand for the product class, and later selective demand for its brand.
concepts.example: When an Edmonton firm launches the first app-controlled snow-melting driveway mat, it advertises heavily to explain what the product is, sells it through only a few retailers, and earns little or no profit.
concepts.contrast: Introduction vs growth: in introduction there are FEW competitors and the objective is AWARENESS; in growth MORE competitors enter, repeat buyers appear and the objective shifts to PRODUCT DIFFERENTIATION.
concepts.trap: 'Create awareness and stimulate trial' is the introduction signal. Skimming OR penetration pricing both belong to introduction, so don't let 'low price' push you to decline ('very low prices') or maturity ('frequent discounts').
concepts.mnemonic: Introduction = 'Hello, world': awareness, trial, few rivals, little profit.

concepts.definition: Primary demand is the desire for the product class rather than for a specific brand; selective demand is the desire for a specific brand within the product class.
concepts.explain: When a product category is brand new, consumers don't yet want the category at all, so the pioneer must first sell the idea of the product class (primary demand). As competitors enter and the category becomes familiar, marketing shifts to persuading buyers to choose one brand over the others (selective demand). In the introduction stage the firm stimulates primary demand first and selective demand later.
concepts.example: Early ads for oat milk explained why anyone would drink oat milk at all (primary demand); today oat-milk brands argue that their brand tastes better or is more sustainable than rivals (selective demand).
concepts.contrast: Primary = 'buy this KIND of product'; selective = 'buy OUR brand of it'. Don't confuse selective demand with selective distribution (a place decision) or with brand loyalty (the maturity-stage objective).
concepts.trap: A pioneering firm explaining what a new category does = primary demand. If the ad compares brands or stresses points of difference versus rivals, it is selective demand.
concepts.mnemonic: Primary = Product class first; Selective = Specific brand second.

concepts.definition: The second PLC stage, marked by rapidly increasing sales, the entry of more competitors, repeat purchasers and an objective of product differentiation; profits increase and reach their maximum.
concepts.explain: Word spreads, early buyers become repeat buyers, and sales climb fast. Competitors see the opportunity and enter, so the firm differentiates: it introduces more features and versions, slowly reduces prices, increases distribution, and its promotion emphasizes points of difference versus the competition. Profits increase and reach their peak late in this stage.
concepts.example: As e-bikes caught on in Canada, early brands added longer-range batteries and cargo versions, expanded from specialty shops into big sporting-goods chains, and advertised what made their bike better than the new rivals.
concepts.contrast: Growth vs maturity: growth = MORE competitors entering, distribution INCREASED, prices SLOWLY REDUCED, profits REACH their maximum; maturity = MANY competitors, FULL distribution, FREQUENT discounts, profits LEVEL OFF.
concepts.trap: Profits PEAK in growth (per the course table), even though sales keep rising into maturity. 'Emphasize points of difference versus the competition' is growth's promotion, not introduction's (awareness) or maturity's (pricing and sales promotion).
concepts.mnemonic: Growth = 'Get different': more features, more rivals, more stores, max profit.

concepts.definition: The third PLC stage, when sales growth slows and sales peak, many competitors fight for share, marginal competitors drop out and the objective is brand loyalty; profits are maximized and level off.
concepts.explain: Most people who will buy the product already have, so growth comes from taking share. With many competitors, firms try to hold market share and build brand loyalty: they ensure the full product line is available and innovative (often adding line extensions), use price discounts frequently, achieve full distribution and promote through pricing and sales promotion. Profits level off and eventually start to decline. Most PLC extension strategies are used here.
concepts.example: Canadian soft drinks are mature: the big brands offer many flavours and sizes, are sold everywhere from Loblaws to gas stations, and constantly run flyer deals.
concepts.contrast: Maturity vs decline: maturity = MANY competitors and FREQUENT discounts with FULL distribution; decline = competitors LEAVING, VERY LOW prices, REDUCED distribution and minimal promotion.
concepts.trap: 'Full distribution is achieved' and 'price discounts are used frequently' are maturity cues. 'Brand loyalty' is maturity's objective, so don't pick growth (product differentiation). Sales peak in maturity, while profits peaked in growth and level off here.
concepts.mnemonic: Maturity = 'Many rivals, loyal fans, everywhere, always on sale.'

concepts.definition: The final PLC stage, when sales fall (usually because of environmental change or new technology), competition is reduced as some competitors leave, and the objective is product rationalization.
concepts.explain: When a better technology or changing tastes arrive, sales drop. Firms rationalize: they retain only best sellers or discontinue items, cut prices very low, reduce distribution and do only minimal promotion, if any. Profits are decreasing and minimal. Management then chooses between deletion (drop the product) and harvesting (keep it with reduced support).
concepts.example: DVD players declined as streaming took over; the remaining makers trimmed their lines to a couple of models, sold them at very low prices and stopped advertising.
concepts.contrast: Decline vs maturity: both involve price pressure, but maturity uses FREQUENT DISCOUNTS while many competitors fight; decline has VERY LOW PRICES while competitors EXIT and distribution SHRINKS. Decline vs introduction: introduction has FEW competitors that EXIST; decline has REDUCED competition as rivals LEAVE.
concepts.trap: 'Product rationalization' is the decline objective; don't confuse it with 'brand loyalty' (maturity). 'Reduced competition' signals decline, not introduction ('few competitors exist').
concepts.mnemonic: Decline = 'Drop or milk': trim the line, slash the price, shrink the shelves.

concepts.definition: Deletion is dropping a product from the company's product line; harvesting is keeping the product but reducing marketing support (and costs) to reap some minor profits from the remaining sales.
concepts.explain: Both are decline-stage strategies. Deletion removes the product completely, freeing resources for better opportunities. Harvesting keeps selling to remaining buyers while cutting promotion and other costs, so each remaining sale is more profitable even as volume shrinks.
concepts.example: A Winnipeg snack maker drops its slow-selling sour-cream crisps entirely (deletion) but keeps its old-fashioned toffee on shelves with no advertising because a loyal base still buys it (harvesting).
concepts.contrast: Harvesting KEEPS the product and CUTS support; deletion DROPS the product. Neither is a PLC extension strategy: extension strategies (product or market modification, repositioning, a new product) try to sustain or revive sales, while harvesting accepts the decline.
concepts.trap: Harvesting cues: 'drastically reduces promotion', 'maximize the remaining profit', 'keeps the product'. Deletion cues: 'discontinue', 'drop from the line', 'remove'. Distractors on the official question are line extension, radical innovation and commercialization.
concepts.mnemonic: Harvest = keep the crop, stop the watering. Delete = pull it out.

concepts.definition: A product for which significant consumer education is required, resulting in an extended introductory period in the PLC.
concepts.explain: If consumers must learn what a product is, how to use it and why it's better, sales take a long time to build, so the introduction stage stretches out. Marketers spend heavily on education before growth kicks in.
concepts.example: When the Swiffer Sweeper first launched, consumers had to understand the new product, how to use it and what to do with their old brooms and mops. Early microwave ovens and electric vehicles are other examples.
concepts.contrast: High-learning = LONG introduction because of consumer education; low-learning = SHORT introduction because benefits are self-evident. Both describe the PLC SHAPE; they are not the degree-of-innovation categories (minor, continuous, radical).
concepts.trap: The stem describes consumers needing to learn how to use something, then asks what 'type of product' it is in PLC terms. Don't pick 'fad' or vague options like 'learning' or 'new concept'. If the question asks about degree of INNOVATION instead, the answer set is minor/continuous/radical.
concepts.mnemonic: High learning = high hurdle = long launch.

concepts.definition: A product whose benefits are self-evident and requires little learning, so it has a short introductory stage and sales begin immediately.
concepts.explain: Because buyers instantly understand what the product does, it skips the long education phase and sales start right away. The downside is that such products are easily copied by competitors, so the firm needs strong, broad distribution to win share quickly.
concepts.example: Dr. Oetker's new frozen pizza flavours sell well immediately with very little promotion; a new cereal under a well-known brand behaves the same way.
concepts.contrast: Low-learning vs high-learning: SHORT introduction and immediate sales vs EXTENDED introduction and heavy education. Low-learning is about PLC SHAPE; the same product judged on degree of innovation would be a MINOR innovation.
concepts.trap: 'Sells well immediately with very little promotion' = low-learning for a PLC-shape question. Don't choose 'fashion' or 'fad': a fad also rises quickly, but its defining feature is the rapid FALL.
concepts.mnemonic: Low learning = little lag.

concepts.definition: A fashion product is a style that becomes popular, declines and then returns in cycles over the years; a fad is a product with a rapid rise and an equally rapid fall, giving it a very short life cycle.
concepts.explain: Both have unusual PLC shapes. Fashions are cyclical: a style falls out of favour and comes back years later. Fads explode in popularity and disappear almost as quickly, usually without returning.
concepts.example: Fidget spinners and the Pet Rock were fads; wide-leg jeans and retro sneaker styles are fashions that keep coming back.
concepts.contrast: Fashion = comes BACK (cyclical, over years); fad = up fast and DOWN fast (very short life, no comeback). A low-learning product also starts fast, but it can enjoy a long life afterward.
concepts.trap: 'Reappears', 'returns', 'comes back in style' = fashion. 'Craze', 'sudden spike then collapse', 'gone within a year' = fad. Don't equate 'fashion' with the clothing industry: a clothing item can be a fad.
concepts.mnemonic: Fashion = Frequent comeback; Fad = Fast and finished.

concepts.definition: Four ways marketers can extend a product's life cycle: (1) modifying the product, (2) modifying the market, (3) repositioning the product and (4) introducing a new product.
concepts.explain: Rather than accept decline, a firm can change the product itself (improvements, line extensions), change who buys it or how it is used (new customers, more use, new use situations), change how it is positioned and the value it offers (repositioning, trading up or down), or replace it with a new product. These strategies are typically used in late growth and maturity.
concepts.example: Arm & Hammer extended the life of its baking soda by promoting a new use situation (deodorizing the fridge) rather than just baking.
concepts.contrast: Extension strategies try to SUSTAIN or REVIVE sales; harvesting and deletion are decline-stage strategies that ACCEPT falling sales. Don't confuse them with the strategic approaches to growth (Ansoff matrix), which classify growth by product and market newness.
concepts.trap: Know each tactic's parent bucket: product improvements and line extensions = MODIFYING THE PRODUCT; new customers, increased use and new use situations = MODIFYING THE MARKET; trading up and trading down = REPOSITIONING.
concepts.mnemonic: P-M-R-N: 'Please Make Revenue Now' (Product, Market, Reposition, New product).

figure.title: Four PLC extension strategies
items: 1. Modifying the product: product improvements; line extensions
2. Modifying the market: finding new customers; increasing a product's use; creating a new use situation
3. Repositioning a product: meet changing consumer needs, react to competition or improve value (trading up / trading down)
4. Introducing a new product

concepts.definition: A PLC extension strategy that alters a product's characteristics, such as its quality, performance or appearance, to increase sales; product improvements and line extensions are its two forms.
concepts.explain: Here the firm changes the PRODUCT, not the market. A product improvement upgrades the existing item (a better formula, longer battery life, a new design) so it stays competitive. A line extension adds a new variety, flavour or size to the existing line. Both aim to keep a mature product fresh.
concepts.example: A Canadian detergent brand reformulates its existing liquid to clean better in cold water and relaunches it as 'new and improved', which is a product improvement.
concepts.contrast: A product improvement modifies an EXISTING item; a line extension ADDS a new item to the line; market modification leaves the product alone and changes WHO uses it or HOW/WHEN it is used.
concepts.trap: If the product itself is unchanged and only the label recipes or the target customer change, it is MARKET modification, not a product improvement. The official soup-recipe question uses 'product improvements' as a distractor.
concepts.mnemonic: Improve the item or extend the line: either way you're changing the PRODUCT.

concepts.definition: The addition of a new item, such as a new flavour, size, variety or model, to an already existing product line under the same brand.
concepts.explain: Line extensions are a product-modification strategy used heavily in maturity: they keep a brand fresh, fill shelf space and meet varied needs. Because the brand is already known and trusted, new items usually require little learning and sell quickly. The risk is that too many varieties confuse consumers and cannibalize the brand's existing items, which is the point of the slide asking 'Why all the varieties? Good idea?' about Tide.
concepts.example: Kellogg's adds two new cereals to its well-known brands and sells over 3 million units in the first quarter because consumers already trust the name.
concepts.contrast: Line extension = a new item in the SAME product line and category; brand extension (Chapter 7) = an existing brand name moved into a NEW product class; product improvement = changing an EXISTING item rather than adding one.
concepts.trap: Line-extension scenarios come with distractors like test marketing, harvesting or dumping. If the brand enters a totally different category (a cereal brand launching frozen pizza), think brand extension, not line extension.
concepts.mnemonic: Line extension = longer line, same brand, same category.

concepts.definition: When a new product takes sales away from the firm's own existing products rather than from competitors.
concepts.explain: If a company launches something its own customers buy INSTEAD of its current products, total company sales barely grow. Cannibalization is a key risk of adding too many line extensions, because new varieties mostly pull buyers from the brand's existing varieties.
concepts.example: When a snack brand launches a 'lightly salted' version of its chips, many buyers simply switch from its regular chips, so the new item mostly eats into the company's own sales.
concepts.contrast: Cannibalization = sales shifted from the firm's OWN products; normal competition = sales taken from or lost to RIVALS. A line extension is the action; cannibalization is a possible consequence.
concepts.trap: 'Sales of the company's existing product fell after it launched its own new version' = cannibalization, not the decline stage or harvesting. The cause is the firm's own new product, not an outside technology change or a competitor.
concepts.mnemonic: Cannibal = eating your own.

concepts.definition: A PLC extension strategy that changes the market for a product rather than the product itself, by finding new customers, increasing a product's use, or creating a new use situation.
concepts.explain: Finding new customers means selling the same product to a group that did not buy it before. Increasing a product's use means getting existing customers to use it more often or in larger amounts. Creating a new use situation means promoting a new occasion or purpose for the product.
concepts.example: Suzanne's Soup Company added dinner recipes to its labels so people would eat its soup at dinner, not just lunch (a new use situation); Arm & Hammer promoting baking soda as a fridge deodorizer is another new use situation.
concepts.contrast: New use situation = a new OCCASION or PURPOSE; increasing use = the SAME use more OFTEN or in larger amounts; finding new customers = a new GROUP of buyers. Product modification, by contrast, changes the product itself.
concepts.trap: Recipes on labels and 'use it for X too' = new use situation, not increasing use. 'Three cans a day instead of one' = increasing use. 'Market our baby shampoo to adults' = finding new customers.
concepts.mnemonic: Who, how much, what for: new customers (who), increased use (how much), new use situation (what for).

figure.title: Three market modifications
items: Finding new customers: a new group of users for the unchanged product
Increasing a product's use: current users use it more often or in larger amounts
Creating a new use situation: a new occasion or purpose for the product

concepts.term: Repositioning (incl. trading up and trading down)
concepts.definition: Changing the place a product occupies in consumers' minds relative to competing products, in order to meet changing consumer needs, react to competition or improve value; it includes trading up and trading down.
concepts.explain: A firm may reposition to react to a competitor's position, reach a new market, catch a rising trend or change the value it offers. Trading up adds value (features, higher quality) and raises the price. Trading down reduces features, quality or price, and also includes downsizing package contents while keeping the price the same.
concepts.example: A Quebec cheese maker repositions its mild cheddar from a kids' lunchbox snack to a premium charcuterie-board cheese with new packaging and a higher price (trading up).
concepts.contrast: Repositioning changes the product's POSITION and value in consumers' minds; product modification changes the PRODUCT itself (an improvement or a new item in the line); market modification targets new users or uses. Trading up = more for more; trading down = less for less, or less for the same price.
concepts.trap: Shrinking package contents at the same price is trading DOWN, not a product improvement. Upgrading an existing item and raising its price is trading UP, not a line extension, unless a separate new item is added to the line.
concepts.mnemonic: Up = more for more; Down = less for less (or less for the same).

concepts.definition: A classification of new products by how much new learning they require of consumers: minor innovations require no new learning, continuous innovations change the consumer's normal routine but do not require totally new learning, and radical innovations require new learning and consumption patterns.
concepts.explain: 'Newness' can be judged from the company's view (new to the firm), the market's view (new to the market) or the consumer's view (how much the consumer must learn). The more learning required, the more the marketing must educate: minor innovations need awareness and wide distribution; continuous innovations need advertising of points of difference and benefits; radical innovations need education through advertising, product trial and personal selling, with public relations playing a major role.
concepts.example: New and improved toothpaste = minor; Swiffer WetJet or wearable technology = continuous; Amazon Alexa, self-driving cars or 3D printers = radical.
concepts.contrast: Degree of innovation classifies the innovation by CONSUMER LEARNING; high- and low-learning describe the SHAPE of the PLC. One product can be both: Dr. Oetker's new pizza flavours are a low-learning product AND a minor innovation.
concepts.trap: 'Continuous improvement' and 'mini updates' are not course terms. 'Changes the routine but not totally new learning' = continuous, not radical. 'Public relations plays a major role', 'personal selling' and 'product trial' = radical. 'Wide distribution' as the emphasis = minor.
concepts.mnemonic: Minor = no learning; Continuous = new routine; Radical = new everything.

concepts.definition: A model of how a new product is adopted over time by five adopter categories: innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%), early majority (34%), late majority (34%) and laggards (16%).
concepts.explain: People don't all buy a new product at once. Venturesome innovators try it first, then early adopters, the leaders in social settings whose approval influences the deliberate early majority. The skeptical late majority follows, and laggards, who fear debt and rely on neighbours and friends for information, come last. Marketers court early adopters because their influence drives the mass market.
concepts.example: When a new smart-ring fitness tracker launches in Toronto, tech enthusiasts who read many review sources buy it first (innovators); popular fitness instructors who post about it are early adopters; most others follow over the next few years.
concepts.contrast: Innovators are VENTURESOME, higher educated and use MULTIPLE information sources; early adopters are LEADERS in social settings with slightly above-average education. Early majority (deliberate, many informal social contacts) vs late majority (skeptical, below-average social status): both are 34%.
concepts.trap: Percentages: 2.5 / 13.5 / 34 / 34 / 16. Laggards are 16%, not 2.5%. Innovators plus early adopters together = 16%; adoption reaches 50% once the early majority has adopted and 84% after the late majority. 'Leaders in social settings' = early adopters, NOT innovators.
concepts.mnemonic: 2.5-13.5-34-34-16: 'Venturesome, Leaders, Deliberate, Skeptical, Debt-fearing.'

concepts.definition: Four barriers that deter consumers from adopting a new product: usage, value, risk and psychological barriers.
concepts.explain: A usage barrier exists when the product isn't compatible with consumers' existing habits. A value barrier exists when the product offers no incentive to switch from what people already use. A risk barrier is the perceived physical, economic or social risk of adopting. A psychological barrier comes from cultural differences or image concerns. Marketers must identify which barrier is at work before they can remove it.
concepts.example: Many Albertans hesitate to buy an electric vehicle because they fear being stranded far from a charger on a cold highway (a risk barrier), even though they understand how to drive one.
concepts.contrast: Usage = 'it doesn't fit how I do things'; value = 'it's not better than what I have'; risk = 'what if it fails, costs me, or embarrasses me'; psychological = 'it clashes with my culture or my image'.
concepts.trap: The four barriers are Usage, Value, Risk and Psychological; 'price', 'distribution' and 'awareness' are not on the list. A cost worry can be a value barrier (not worth switching) or a risk barrier (fear of an expensive mistake), so read the cue words.
concepts.mnemonic: U-V-R-P: 'Useful? Valuable? Risky? Personal?'

concepts.term: NPD challenges and why new products fail
concepts.definition: New products are the lifeblood of a company, but new product development is expensive and risky; new products commonly fail because of an insignificant point of difference, an incomplete new concept definition, insufficient market attractiveness, poor execution of the marketing mix, or bad timing.
concepts.explain: NPD is an expensive undertaking with a high risk of failure, high research costs and extensive time and effort spent on prototypes and marketing materials. A failure means expensive product write-offs (labour, materials and expenses to fix the problem) and a lack of future credibility in the market. Figure 8-7 pairs each failure issue with a solution; for example, an insignificant point of difference is fixed by determining a distinctive, meaningful POD through consumer research and competitor monitoring.
concepts.example: The Amazon Fire Phone, Google Glass, Lululemon's sheer pants and New Coke are notable new-product failures shown in the slides.
concepts.contrast: Insignificant POD (not meaningfully different) vs incomplete concept definition (features, benefits and positioning never clearly defined) vs insufficient market attractiveness (target market too small or not growing) vs poor marketing-mix execution (4 Ps misaligned, weak distribution) vs bad timing (launched when consumers weren't eager or conditions were wrong).
concepts.trap: Match the SOLUTION to the issue: 'identify a target market large enough with growth potential' fixes insufficient market attractiveness; 'align the 4 Ps incl. brand name and package and gain sufficient distribution' fixes poor execution; 'launch when consumers are eager; monitor market conditions and competitors' fixes bad timing.
concepts.mnemonic: Failure causes P-C-M-E-T: POD, Concept, Market, Execution, Timing.

concepts.definition: A matrix that classifies growth strategies by whether the product and the market are current or new: market penetration (current product, current market), product development (new product, current market), market development (current product, new market) and diversification (new product, new market).
concepts.explain: Ask two questions: is the product current or new, and is the market (the customers) current or new? Market penetration finds ways to make current products appeal more to current customers. Product development reaches current customers with a new product. Market development reaches new customers, such as a new segment or a new country, with a current product. Diversification reaches new customers with a new product and carries the most risk because nothing is familiar.
concepts.example: A coffee chain running a loyalty promotion so regulars visit more often is market penetration; adding a new menu item for those regulars is product development; taking its existing menu to a new country is market development; launching an unrelated product for a new market is diversification.
concepts.contrast: Market DEVELOPMENT = current product, NEW market; product DEVELOPMENT = NEW product, current market. The word before 'development' tells you what is new. Adapting an existing product line to a new country's culture is still market development, not product development or diversification.
concepts.trap: Light adaptation of an existing line for a foreign market (the official Yummy Brand question) = market development. Call it diversification only when BOTH the product and the market are genuinely new. Selling more of the same product to the same customers, or winning share from rivals in the same market, = market penetration.
concepts.mnemonic: The word before 'development' names what's NEW. Penetration = nothing new; diversification = everything new.

concepts.definition: The seven sequential steps a firm uses to develop new products: (1) new product development strategy, (2) idea generation, (3) screening and evaluation, (4) business analysis, (5) development, (6) test marketing and (7) commercialization.
concepts.explain: The process works like a funnel: many ideas enter, and at each step weak ideas are eliminated so money is spent only on the most promising ones. The early steps are cheap (strategy, ideas, screening with concept tests); the later steps (prototypes, test markets, full launch) are expensive. Test marketing is done only if necessary.
concepts.example: A Calgary beverage company sets a goal of low-sugar drinks (strategy), collects 120 flavour ideas from staff and customers (idea generation), narrows them to five concepts tested with consumers (screening and evaluation), projects costs and profits (business analysis), brews prototypes (development), sells them only in Lethbridge (test marketing), then launches across Alberta (commercialization).
concepts.contrast: Screening and evaluation narrows ideas and uses CONCEPT TESTS (descriptions); business analysis makes FINANCIAL projections; development builds PROTOTYPES; test marketing sells on a LIMITED scale in defined areas; commercialization is the FULL launch.
concepts.trap: Know the positions: screening and evaluation is step 3; business analysis is step 4 and comes BEFORE development (step 5); test marketing is step 6, BEFORE commercialization. Concept tests happen in screening, not development.
concepts.mnemonic: 'Smart Ideas Survive Business Development Testing Completely': Strategy, Ideas, Screening, Business analysis, Development, Test marketing, Commercialization.

figure.title: Figure 8-9 Steps in the NPD process
items: 1. New product development strategy: identify an NPD focus that meets company objectives (company objectives; SWOT analysis)
2. Idea generation: brainstorm new ideas (employees, co-workers, consumers)
3. Screening and evaluation: evaluate ideas and develop concepts (internal technical evaluation; external concept tests)
4. Business analysis: key features, marketing strategy, financial projections (production, legal, profitability)
5. Development: create and test the prototype internally and with consumers
6. Test marketing: test product and marketing strategy on a limited scale, if necessary
7. Commercialization: launch and fully market the product (all of the marketing mix; possible regional rollout)

concepts.definition: Step 1, new product development strategy, identifies a new-product focus that meets company objectives, using the company's objectives and a SWOT analysis; step 2, idea generation, brainstorms new ideas from sources such as employees, co-workers, consumers, suppliers, competitors, universities and crowdsourcing.
concepts.explain: Before inventing anything, the firm decides what kind of new products fit its goals and strengths (the strategic direction, often framed with the growth matrix). Then it casts a wide net for ideas: employees and co-workers, consumers' suggestions and complaints, suppliers, competitors (through reverse engineering), universities and inventors, and crowdsourcing or open innovation.
concepts.example: A Halifax seafood company reviews its objectives and runs a SWOT analysis showing strength in frozen distribution (strategy), then runs an online contest inviting customers to suggest new frozen meals (idea generation through crowdsourcing).
concepts.contrast: Strategy = deciding the FOCUS (objectives, SWOT); idea generation = BRAINSTORMING many ideas; screening and evaluation = NARROWING those ideas to a manageable list of promising concepts.
concepts.trap: Reverse engineering a competitor's product and crowdsourcing are IDEA GENERATION sources, not screening or development. A SWOT analysis of the company, product or brand belongs to the STRATEGY step, not business analysis.
concepts.mnemonic: First decide WHERE to look (strategy), then look EVERYWHERE (ideas).

concepts.definition: The third NPD step, which internally and externally evaluates new-product ideas to eliminate those that warrant no further effort, reducing the array of brainstormed ideas to a manageable list of promising concepts.
concepts.explain: Internally, the company checks technical requirements and fit. Externally, it runs concept tests: consumers see a description or sketch of the product idea (not an actual product) and say how interested they are. Ideas that fail are dropped cheaply, before money is spent on detailed financials or prototypes.
concepts.example: A Vancouver kitchenware firm shows 300 consumers written descriptions of six gadget ideas and drops the four with the weakest purchase intent.
concepts.contrast: Concept test (screening) = consumers react to a DESCRIPTION of an idea; prototype test (development) = consumers try an actual working MODEL; test market = consumers BUY the finished product in a limited area.
concepts.trap: 'Reduce the array of brainstorming ideas to a manageable list' = screening and evaluation (official question), not idea generation or development. If consumers react to descriptions or drawings, it is a concept test in screening.
concepts.mnemonic: Screen = sieve: lots of ideas in, a few concepts out.

concepts.definition: The fourth NPD step, which specifies the product's key features and anticipated marketing strategy and makes financial projections, assessing production, legal and profitability issues.
concepts.explain: Before spending on prototypes, the firm checks whether the concept makes business sense: what features it will have, how it will be priced, promoted and distributed, what it will cost to produce, whether there are legal issues, and whether it will be profitable.
concepts.example: Before building any prototypes, a Saskatoon agri-tech firm forecasts sales of its soil sensor, estimates production costs, checks for patent conflicts and projects a three-year break-even.
concepts.contrast: Business analysis = paper and spreadsheet work (features, marketing mix, finances, legal); screening and evaluation = narrowing ideas with concept tests; development = building and testing the physical PROTOTYPE.
concepts.trap: 'Financial projections', 'profitability', 'legal issues' and 'production' = business analysis. It comes BEFORE development (step 4 vs step 5), even though some students assume you build first and crunch numbers afterward.
concepts.mnemonic: Business analysis = 'Will it make money?'

concepts.definition: The fifth NPD step, which turns the idea on paper into a prototype and tests it internally at the company and externally with consumers.
concepts.explain: Engineers and designers build working models. Internal company assessments (lab tests of safety, durability and performance) and external tests in which consumers use the prototype make sure the product works and that people like it before it goes anywhere near a store.
concepts.example: A Montreal toy maker builds 50 working prototypes of a coding robot, stress-tests them in its lab and lends them to families for two weeks to gather feedback.
concepts.contrast: Development = consumers test a working PROTOTYPE; concept tests in screening = consumers react only to a DESCRIPTION; test marketing = the finished product is actually SOLD in a limited area.
concepts.trap: Don't confuse the NPD step 'development' with 'product development' in the growth matrix (a new product for current customers) or 'market development' (a current product for new customers). In the NPD process, development means building and testing prototypes.
concepts.mnemonic: Development = 'Make a model and try it.'

concepts.definition: The sixth NPD step: offering a product for sale on a limited basis in a defined area to gauge consumer reactions and test the marketing strategy before a full launch.
concepts.explain: Types include standard test markets (the product is sold in actual cities through regular channels), controlled test markets (retailers are paid to stock and display the product) and simulated or laboratory test markets (consumers see ads and shop in a simulated store). Test marketing is not always necessary: it is expensive, it alerts competitors, and it isn't practical for durable goods.
concepts.example: A packaged-food company sells its new frozen perogies only in Regina and Saskatoon for three months to measure repeat purchases before going national.
concepts.contrast: Test marketing sells the FINISHED product on a LIMITED scale to gather information; commercialization is the FULL-scale launch; development tests PROTOTYPES; a regional rollout (part of commercialization) is a sequenced full launch, not a test.
concepts.trap: Firms may SKIP test marketing when it is too costly, when they don't want to tip off competitors, or for durable goods such as cars or appliances. 'Retailers are paid' = controlled test market; 'simulated store' = simulated test market; 'actual cities, regular channels' = standard test market.
concepts.mnemonic: Test market = 'Try it in Regina before all of Canada.'

concepts.definition: The seventh and final NPD step: positioning and launching a new product in full-scale production and sales with full marketing support, implementing all areas of the marketing mix.
concepts.explain: This is the expensive full launch: production ramps up, the full marketing mix goes live, and the product enters the introduction stage of the PLC. Many firms use a regional rollout, introducing the product sequentially into geographical areas so that production and marketing can build up gradually.
concepts.example: After a successful start in Ontario, a beverage start-up launches its sparkling tea in Quebec in spring, the Prairies in summer and B.C. in fall: a regional rollout during commercialization.
concepts.contrast: Commercialization = FULL-scale launch (possibly region by region); test marketing = LIMITED sale to gather data before deciding whether to launch. A regional rollout is a launch schedule, not a test.
concepts.trap: 'Full-scale production, sales and marketing support' = commercialization (official question). Distractors include concept test, test marketing and business analysis. Commercialization is where the NPD process hands off to the PLC's introduction stage.
concepts.mnemonic: Commercialization = 'Go big, or go region by region.'

activities.title: Order the NPD steps
activities.prompt: Put the seven steps of the new product development process in the correct order.
items: New product development strategy
Idea generation
Screening and evaluation
Business analysis
Development
Test marketing
Commercialization
activities.explanation: The process is a funnel. The firm first sets a strategic focus, then brainstorms ideas, screens them down to a manageable list (concept tests), runs the numbers on the survivors (business analysis), builds and tests prototypes (development), tests the finished product on a limited scale if necessary (test marketing), and finally launches with full marketing support (commercialization). Business analysis comes before development so money isn't spent on prototypes that won't be profitable.

activities.title: Sort into the growth matrix
activities.prompt: Drag each scenario into the correct strategic approach to growth.

A paint store cuts prices on its existing paint to win neighbourhood shoppers from rivals
A bank creates a new travel-insurance product for its current account holders
A yogurt maker adds a new high-protein yogurt for its existing grocery shoppers
A Canadian snack brand adapts its existing line to local tastes and enters Costa Rica
A children's sunscreen brand starts marketing the same sunscreen to adult golfers
A dairy co-operative opens a chain of car washes in a new province
A furniture maker launches electric scooters aimed at university students

activities.explanation: Ask two questions: is the product current or new, and is the market current or new? Same product, same customers = market penetration. New product, same customers = product development. Same product, new customers (a new segment or a new country, even with cultural adaptation) = market development. New product, new customers = diversification.

Price: skimming or penetration, slowly reduced, frequent discounts, very low. Place: limited, increased, full, reduced. Profit: minimal, rising to its maximum (growth), maximized and levelling off (maturity), decreasing (decline).

Innovators are the venturesome risk-takers; early adopters are the leaders in social settings whose influence moves the deliberate early majority; the skeptical late majority follows; laggards fear debt and rely on neighbours and friends.

activities.title: Sort by degree of innovation
activities.prompt: Drag each example, learning requirement or marketing emphasis to its degree of innovation (Figure 8-5).

activities.explanation: The more a consumer must learn, the more the marketing must educate. Minor innovations need no learning, so awareness and wide distribution are enough. Continuous innovations change routines, so ads stress points of difference and benefits. Radical innovations need new consumption patterns, so firms educate through advertising, trial, personal selling and public relations.

activities.title: Match the PLC extension tactic
activities.prompt: Match each PLC extension tactic with the scenario that illustrates it.

pairs.right: A detergent is reformulated to clean better in cold water
Kellogg's adds two new cereals to its well-known brands
A baby shampoo is marketed to adults with sensitive scalps
A sparkling-water brand urges current drinkers to have three cans a day instead of one
Labels on a lunch soup carry dinner recipes
Basic candles get soy wax, designer jars and a higher price
A chip bag shrinks from 235 g to 200 g at the same price
A sixth-generation tablet replaces a fifth generation whose sales have flattened

activities.explanation: Product improvements and line extensions modify the PRODUCT. New customers, increased use and new use situations modify the MARKET (who, how much, and for what). Trading up and trading down are REPOSITIONING moves that change the value offered. Replacing an ageing product with a new one is the fourth strategy, introducing a new product.

questions.stem: The _____ describes the stages a new product goes through in the marketplace and is used to help manage a product from its initial launch to its eventual decline.
questions.explanation: The product life cycle (PLC) tracks a product through introduction, growth, maturity and decline in the marketplace. The adoption curve is tempting, but it describes the categories of PEOPLE who adopt a product over time, not the product's stages.

questions.stem: Over a decade, sales of Northwind's home robot vacuums rose slowly at first, then surged, then flattened once most interested households owned one, and are now falling as a newer technology arrives. Which concept does this pattern illustrate?
questions.explanation: Sales that rise slowly, surge, flatten and then fall trace the four PLC stages: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. It is not a fad, which rises and collapses rapidly over a very short life rather than over a decade.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the timing of the sales and profit curves in the product life cycle?
options: Profits reach their maximum in growth, while sales peak in maturity
Sales and profits both reach their peak in the maturity stage
Sales peak in growth, while profits peak in maturity
Profits peak in introduction because there are few competitors
questions.explanation: Per Figure 8-3, growth brings 'increased profits that reach their maximum' and maturity brings 'maximized profits that level off', while sales keep rising until they peak in maturity. The 'both peak in maturity' option is the classic mistake: profits top out earlier, late in growth.

questions.stem: Technology products tend to have longer product life cycles than most other products because consumers need time to learn how to use them.
questions.explanation: False. The length of the PLC varies by product, and technology products tend to have SHORTER life cycles because newer technology quickly replaces them. Corrected statement: technology products tend to have shorter PLCs.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly lists the stages of the product life cycle?
questions.explanation: The PLC runs introduction, growth, maturity, decline. A common slip is putting maturity before growth; sales must grow rapidly before they can level off in maturity.

questions.stem: Which statement about the PLC profit curve (Figure 8-1) is NOT true?
options: Profit is negative or minimal during the introduction stage
Profits reach their peak at the same moment sales peak
Profits increase and reach their maximum during growth
Profits decrease to minimal levels in the decline stage
questions.explanation: Profits peak late in the growth stage and then level off in maturity, while sales peak later, in maturity. So profits and sales do NOT peak at the same moment; the other three statements match the course's profit row.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the general marketing objective in each PLC stage, from introduction to decline?
options: Awareness, product differentiation, brand loyalty, product rationalization
Awareness, brand loyalty, product differentiation, product rationalization
Product differentiation, awareness, brand loyalty, product rationalization
Awareness, product differentiation, product rationalization, brand loyalty
questions.explanation: Figure 8-3's objective row is awareness (introduction), product differentiation (growth), brand loyalty (maturity), product rationalization (decline). Swapping differentiation and loyalty is the classic error: you differentiate while competitors are still entering, then defend with loyalty once the market is crowded.

questions.stem: Across the PLC, how does distribution (place) change from introduction to decline according to Figure 8-3?
questions.explanation: The place row reads: limited distribution (introduction), distribution is increased (growth), full distribution is achieved (maturity), distribution is reduced (decline). Full distribution is not reached until maturity, so 'limited, full, increased' is wrong.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a PLC stage with a Figure 8-3 entry is INCORRECT?
options: Introduction, price: use a skimming or penetration strategy
Growth, place: full distribution is achieved
Maturity, promotion: focus on pricing and sales promotion
Decline, product: retain only best sellers or discontinue
questions.explanation: In growth, distribution is INCREASED; full distribution is achieved only in maturity. The other three pairings are exactly as the table lists them.

questions.stem: A classmate made four flashcards from Figure 8-3. Which card contains an error?
options: Growth, profit: increased profits that reach their maximum
Decline, promotion: only minimal promotion, if any
questions.explanation: Maturity's general marketing objective is brand loyalty; product differentiation is the growth objective. The other three cards are correct, including growth as the stage where profits reach their maximum.

questions.stem: One row of Figure 8-3 reads 'focus on building awareness with advertising' in introduction and 'emphasize points of difference versus the competition' in growth. Which row is it?
questions.explanation: These are promotion entries; the row continues with 'focus on pricing and sales promotion' (maturity) and 'only minimal promotion, if any' (decline). The objective row is tempting because it uses related ideas, but its entries are single terms: awareness, product differentiation, brand loyalty, product rationalization.

questions.stem: A brand manager learns that her product's general marketing objective is now 'product rationalization'. Which set of actions fits that stage?
options: Introduce more features, slowly reduce prices, increase distribution, stress points of difference
Ensure a full line, use frequent discounts, achieve full distribution, focus on sales promotion
Retain only best sellers, use very low prices, reduce distribution, keep promotion minimal
Focus on a new brand, use skimming, limit distribution, advertise for awareness
questions.explanation: Product rationalization is the decline-stage objective, so the matching column is: retain only best sellers or discontinue, very low prices, reduced distribution and minimal promotion. The full-line and frequent-discount option describes maturity, whose objective is brand loyalty.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'In maturity, promotion emphasizes points of difference versus the competition.' Which correction is accurate?
options: Maturity promotion focuses on pricing and sales promotion; emphasizing points of difference belongs to growth
Maturity promotion focuses on building awareness with advertising; points of difference belong to decline
Maturity promotion is minimal, if any; points of difference belong to introduction
No correction is needed; maturity promotion emphasizes points of difference
questions.explanation: In Figure 8-3, growth promotion emphasizes points of difference versus competitors (matching its product differentiation objective), while maturity promotion focuses on pricing and sales promotion. Minimal promotion belongs to decline, and awareness advertising to introduction.

questions.stem: In Figure 8-3, the profit row reads: minimal profits, if any (introduction); increased profits that reach their maximum (growth); maximized profits that level off (maturity); decreasing and minimal profits (decline).
questions.explanation: True. This is the exact profit row. Profits reach their maximum in growth and then level off in maturity, which is why 'profits peak in maturity' is a trap.

questions.stem: Why does Figure 8-3 show 'reduced competition, with some competitors leaving the market' in the decline stage?
options: Strong brand loyalty built in maturity blocks new rivals from entering
Patents earned during development prevent competitors from selling
Full distribution leaves no shelf space for additional competitors
Falling sales and minimal profits make the market unattractive, so some firms exit
questions.explanation: In decline, sales fall (often because of new technology or environmental change) and profits become decreasing and minimal, so some competitors leave. Brand loyalty is the maturity objective and does not explain why rivals exit in decline.

questions.stem: Cybrex is in the business of making software packages for tax purposes. It is in the _____ stage if its marketing objective is to create consumer awareness and stimulate trial for its new software packages.
questions.explanation: The marketing objective in the introduction stage is to create consumer awareness and stimulate trial for the new product (Figure 8-3 lists awareness as the introduction objective). Growth is tempting, but by then the objective has shifted to product differentiation as more competitors enter.

questions.stem: Solaris Shades has just launched a patented self-tinting window film, the first of its kind in Canada, and must set its initial price. According to Figure 8-3, which pricing approach fits this stage?
options: Prices slowly reduced as rivals enter
Frequent price discounts to hold share
Very low prices to clear remaining stock
questions.explanation: A just-launched product is in introduction, where Figure 8-3 says to use a skimming (high price to recover R&D) or penetration (low price to build volume) strategy. 'Prices slowly reduced' is the growth-stage entry, after competitors begin to enter.

questions.stem: Why are profits typically minimal, if any, during the introduction stage?
options: Sales are still low while R&D and launch advertising costs are high
Intense competition forces the firm into frequent price discounts
Full distribution pushes channel and shipping costs to their peak
Very low prices are used to clear out the remaining inventory
questions.explanation: In introduction, few people know the product, so sales are low, while the firm is still recovering R&D and spending heavily on awareness advertising. Intense competition and frequent discounts describe maturity, not introduction, where few competitors exist.

questions.stem: Which pair of characteristics best distinguishes the introduction stage from the growth stage?
options: Many competitors and full distribution vs reduced competition and reduced distribution
Brand loyalty objective vs product rationalization objective
Few competitors and limited distribution vs more competitors entering and increased distribution
Frequent price discounts vs very low prices
questions.explanation: Introduction has few competitors and limited distribution; in growth, more competitors enter and distribution is increased. The other pairs compare maturity with decline, not introduction with growth.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT typical of the introduction stage?
options: Advertising focused on building awareness of the new product
Limited distribution through a few selected retailers
A focus on introducing a new product or brand
Promotion that emphasizes points of difference versus the competition
questions.explanation: Emphasizing points of difference versus competitors is the growth-stage promotion, used once rivals have entered. Introduction promotion focuses on building awareness with advertising, because there are few competitors to compare against.

questions.stem: In the introduction stage, the general marketing objective is product differentiation.
questions.explanation: False. The introduction objective is awareness: create consumer awareness and stimulate trial. Product differentiation is the growth-stage objective, when more competitors enter the market.

questions.stem: The desire for a product class, rather than for a specific brand, is called:
questions.explanation: Primary demand is demand for the product class as a whole, which a pioneer must build first in the introduction stage. Selective demand is the opposite: demand for a specific brand within the class.

questions.stem: Ferment Co., the first company to sell kombucha in Atlantic Canada, runs ads explaining what kombucha is and why fermented tea is good for you, without comparing its brand to any other. These ads aim to stimulate:
questions.explanation: Explaining what a new product category is and why to buy it at all builds primary demand, the first task in the introduction stage. Selective demand would require persuading buyers to choose Ferment Co. over competing brands, which these ads don't do.

questions.stem: Eight kombucha brands now crowd Atlantic Canadian shelves. Ferment Co., the category pioneer, changes its ads from explaining what kombucha is to stressing that its tea is organic and locally brewed, unlike rivals. The ads have shifted from stimulating:
questions.explanation: The early ads built primary demand (desire for the kombucha category); now that competitors exist, the ads build selective demand (desire for Ferment Co.'s brand specifically). The reverse order is wrong: a pioneer moves from primary to selective demand.

questions.stem: According to the textbook, how should a pioneering firm sequence its demand-building efforts in the introduction stage?
options: Stimulate selective demand first, then primary demand
Stimulate only selective demand, since the category is already known
Stimulate any demand only after the growth stage begins
Stimulate primary demand first, then later selective demand
questions.explanation: In introduction, the firm must first stimulate primary demand (for the product class) and later selective demand (for its brand). Consumers can't prefer a brand of a product class they don't yet want, so selective demand comes second.

questions.stem: A company that is the only seller in a brand-new product category gains little from ads comparing its brand with rivals; its first task is to build primary demand.
questions.explanation: True. With no rivals and an unfamiliar category, the firm must first create desire for the product class itself (primary demand). Brand-versus-brand messages build selective demand, which matters once competitors enter.

questions.stem: Sales of PeakTrail's avalanche beacons are climbing quickly, and many buyers are now repeat purchasers. Several new rivals have entered, so PeakTrail is adding features, slowly lowering prices and getting into more stores. Which PLC stage is PeakTrail in?
questions.explanation: Rapidly rising sales, repeat purchasers, more competitors entering, more features, slowly reduced prices and increased distribution are all growth-stage signs. Maturity is tempting, but maturity has many established competitors, full distribution and frequent discounts rather than slowly falling prices.

questions.stem: Rivals have started copying VoltPup's popular dog-walking e-collar, and sales are rising rapidly. According to Figure 8-3, what should VoltPup's promotion focus on now?
options: Emphasizing points of difference versus the competition
Building awareness of the product with advertising
Focusing on pricing and frequent sales promotions
Keeping promotion to a minimum, if any at all
questions.explanation: Competitors entering plus rapidly rising sales signals growth, where promotion emphasizes points of difference versus the competition. Building awareness was the introduction-stage focus; pricing and sales promotion is the maturity-stage focus.

questions.stem: In the growth stage of the PLC, the general marketing objective is _____.
questions.explanation: Growth's objective is product differentiation, because new competitors are entering and the firm must stand apart. Brand loyalty is the maturity objective, used once the market is crowded and the goal shifts to holding share.

questions.stem: Two products are both profitable. Product A's distribution is still being increased and its profits are rising to their maximum. Product B has full distribution and maximized profits that have levelled off. Which is correct?
options: A is in maturity; B is in growth
A is in introduction; B is in growth
Both are in maturity because both are profitable
A is in growth; B is in maturity
questions.explanation: Increasing distribution and profits that reach their maximum are growth entries; full distribution and maximized profits that level off are maturity entries. Being profitable does not by itself place a product in maturity.

questions.stem: Why do more competitors typically enter the market during the growth stage?
options: Rapidly rising sales and profits signal an attractive opportunity
Sales have levelled off, so firms compete mainly on price
The pioneering firm has stopped advertising
Consumers have lost interest in the product class
questions.explanation: In growth, sales climb rapidly and profits rise toward their maximum, which attracts rivals. Levelled-off sales describe maturity, by which point many competitors are already in the market.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a growth-stage characteristic?
options: Repeat purchasers begin to appear in the market
More features and versions of the product are introduced
Profits increase and reach their maximum level
Price discounts are used frequently to hold market share
questions.explanation: Frequent price discounts to hold share are a maturity-stage tactic; in growth, prices are only slowly reduced. Repeat purchasers, added features and peak profits are all growth characteristics.

questions.stem: Canadian frozen-pizza brands are sold in nearly every grocery store, offer dozens of varieties and fight for share with weekly flyer discounts. Sales growth has slowed and a few small brands have dropped out. Which PLC stage is this category in?
questions.explanation: Full distribution, a full product line, frequent price discounts, slowing sales growth and marginal competitors dropping out are maturity signs. It is not decline: competition is still intense and distribution is full rather than reduced.

questions.stem: Figure 8-3 lists _____ as the general marketing objective of the maturity stage.
questions.explanation: Maturity's objective is brand loyalty: with many competitors and slowing growth, firms focus on holding market share. Product differentiation is the earlier growth objective.

questions.stem: Brewster Coffee's bagged coffee faces many competitors and already has full distribution across Canada. Which action best fits its PLC stage according to Figure 8-3?
options: Cut distribution and keep only the best-selling items in the line
Use frequent price discounts and sales promotion while keeping a full product line
Focus advertising on building awareness of the product category
Slowly reduce prices while expanding into more retail stores
questions.explanation: Many competitors plus full distribution means maturity, where firms ensure the full product line is available and innovative, use frequent price discounts and focus promotion on pricing and sales promotion. Slowly reducing prices while expanding distribution is the growth-stage pattern.

questions.stem: What best distinguishes the maturity stage from the decline stage in Figure 8-3?
options: Maturity: very low prices and reduced distribution; decline: frequent discounts and full distribution
Maturity: few competitors; decline: many competitors
Maturity: profits reach their maximum; decline: profits level off
Maturity: frequent price discounts and full distribution; decline: very low prices and reduced distribution
questions.explanation: Maturity uses frequent price discounts with full distribution; decline uses very low prices with reduced distribution. The profit option is wrong because maturity's profits are maximized and level off, while decline's are decreasing and minimal.

questions.stem: Why are most PLC extension strategies, such as line extensions and finding new customers, applied during the maturity stage?
options: Sales growth has slowed and many rivals fight for share, so new sources of sales are needed
Profits are still negative, so the firm must recover its R&D costs quickly
Distribution is still limited, so the firm needs to recruit many more retailers
Consumers do not yet understand what the product class does or why to buy it
questions.explanation: In maturity, most potential buyers already own the product and many competitors fight over them, so firms modify the product, the market or the positioning to keep sales from sliding into decline. Negative profits and limited distribution describe introduction, not maturity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT characteristic of the maturity stage?
options: Marginal competitors drop out of the market
Firms focus on holding market share
Distribution is reduced to cut costs
Line extensions fill out the product line
questions.explanation: Reduced distribution belongs to decline; in maturity, full distribution is achieved. Marginal competitors dropping out, holding market share and adding line extensions are all maturity features.

questions.stem: Sales of HomeFax's desktop fax machines are falling as businesses switch to e-signatures. Two rivals have exited the market, HomeFax has cut its line to its two best sellers, and it sells them at very low prices through fewer retailers with no advertising. Which PLC stage is this?
questions.explanation: Sales falling because of a new technology, competitors exiting, a line trimmed to best sellers, very low prices, fewer retailers and no advertising are all decline entries in Figure 8-3. Maturity also involves price pressure, but there discounts are frequent while distribution stays full.

questions.stem: Sales in the decline stage typically fall because of environmental change or new technology, such as the arrival of a better substitute.
questions.explanation: True. Decline is usually triggered by outside change, such as streaming replacing DVDs. This differs from cannibalization, where the firm's own new product takes sales from its existing products.

questions.stem: Both the introduction and decline stages can show few competitors and modest marketing activity. Which pair of cues tells them apart?
options: Introduction: few competitors exist; decline: some competitors are leaving
Introduction: limited distribution; decline: full distribution
Introduction: very low prices; decline: skimming prices
Introduction: brand loyalty objective; decline: awareness objective
questions.explanation: Introduction has few competitors because the market is new; decline has reduced competition because rivals are leaving a shrinking market. The distribution option is wrong because decline has REDUCED distribution, not full distribution.

questions.stem: Skyline Audio's portable CD players are in the decline stage. Following Figure 8-3, what should its product strategy be?
options: Introduce more features to differentiate from rivals
Ensure the full product line is available and innovative
Retain only the best sellers or discontinue the line
Focus on launching the product as a new brand
questions.explanation: Figure 8-3's decline product entry is 'retain only best sellers or discontinue', matching the product rationalization objective. Ensuring a full, innovative line is the maturity entry, and introducing more features is the growth entry.

questions.stem: Which practice is NOT part of the decline stage in Figure 8-3?
options: Very low prices on the remaining items
Frequent price discounts to build brand loyalty
Only minimal promotion, if any at all
questions.explanation: Frequent price discounts aimed at brand loyalty are maturity tactics. In decline, prices are very low, distribution is reduced and promotion is minimal, if any, because the objective is product rationalization.

questions.stem: Simon Watercraft expects, and starts to see, decreasing profits for its product line of water ski boats. In response, the company drastically reduces promotional activities to maximize the remaining profit from the remaining sales. This strategy is known as:
questions.explanation: Harvesting means keeping the product but reducing marketing support to reap some minor profits during the decline stage, which is exactly what Simon does by slashing promotion. A line extension adds a new item to a line, the opposite of cutting support.

questions.stem: Dropping a product from the company's product line is called:
questions.explanation: Deletion removes the product from the line entirely. Harvesting is the tempting distractor, but harvesting KEEPS the product and simply cuts its marketing support.

questions.stem: Maple Grove Foods discontinues its canned lima beans and removes them from its catalogue so it can put those resources into its growing frozen-meal line. This decline-stage strategy is:
questions.explanation: Discontinuing a product and removing it from the line is deletion. Harvesting would keep the lima beans on sale with reduced marketing support to collect the remaining profit.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between harvesting and deletion?
options: Harvesting keeps the product but cuts support; deletion drops it from the line
Harvesting drops the product; deletion keeps it with reduced support
Harvesting is used in the maturity stage; deletion is used in the growth stage
Harvesting adds new varieties to the line; deletion removes the old varieties
questions.explanation: Both are decline-stage strategies: harvesting keeps the product and reduces marketing support to reap minor profits, while deletion removes it from the line. The option claiming harvesting drops the product simply reverses the two definitions, a common mix-up.

questions.stem: Why might a firm choose harvesting rather than deletion for a declining product?
options: Harvesting revives sales growth by repositioning the product for new buyers
Some loyal buyers remain, so cutting costs still yields minor profits from remaining sales
Harvesting is a required step before a product can be test marketed again
Deletion is only allowed for products that never reached the maturity stage
questions.explanation: Harvesting makes sense when enough buyers remain that a low-cost, low-support product still throws off some profit. It does not revive sales; reviving sales is the goal of PLC extension strategies such as repositioning.

questions.stem: Brava Cosmetics is harvesting its old line of compact powder. Which action would be INCONSISTENT with a harvesting strategy?
options: Cutting its advertising budget to almost nothing
Keeping the product available for loyal buyers
Reducing the number of retailers that carry it
Launching a national ad campaign to revive sales
questions.explanation: Harvesting means reducing marketing support, so a national campaign to revive sales contradicts it (that would be an attempt to extend the PLC). Cutting ads, keeping the product for loyal buyers and trimming distribution all fit harvesting.

questions.stem: When the Swiffer Sweeper was first introduced it required consumers to understand the new product, how to use it, and what to do with their old brooms and mops. This is an example of a _____ product.
questions.explanation: A high-learning product has an extended introductory period because significant effort is required to educate consumers on its usage and benefits, exactly the Swiffer Sweeper situation. A fad is wrong because a fad is defined by a rapid rise and rapid fall, not by consumer education.

questions.stem: A product that requires significant consumer education, and therefore has an extended introductory period, is a:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a high-learning product. A low-learning product is the opposite: its benefits are self-evident, so the introduction is short and sales begin immediately.

questions.stem: When induction cooktops first appeared in Canadian stores, buyers had to learn that only magnetic pans work, how the touch controls respond and why the surface stays cool. Sales took years to build. In PLC terms, induction cooktops were a:
questions.explanation: Needing to learn about new cookware, controls and benefits stretched out the introductory period, the mark of a high-learning product. A low-learning product would have sold immediately because its benefits are self-evident.

questions.stem: The Swiffer Sweeper is a classic high-learning product, yet Figure 8-5 lists the Swiffer WetJet as a continuous innovation. How can both classifications be valid?
options: High-learning is a PLC shape (long introduction); continuous innovation rates how much routines change
They contradict each other, so the WetJet must really be classed as a radical innovation
High-learning and continuous innovation are simply two names for the same concept
High-learning refers to the firm's own production learning curve, not to consumers
questions.explanation: The two frameworks answer different questions. High- vs low-learning describes the SHAPE of the PLC (how long introduction lasts), while minor/continuous/radical classifies the innovation by how much consumer learning it involves; changing routines without totally new learning is continuous. They are not synonyms.

questions.stem: Vireo Mobility is launching a home exoskeleton that users must learn to put on, calibrate and trust before they will rely on it. What PLC pattern should Vireo plan for?
options: Immediate sales with very little promotion needed
A rapid rise in sales followed by a rapid fall
Sales that rise, fade away and return in later cycles
An extended introductory period requiring heavy consumer education
questions.explanation: A product that requires significant consumer learning is a high-learning product, so Vireo should budget for a long introduction stage focused on education. Immediate sales with little promotion describes a low-learning product.

questions.stem: Dr. Oetker, a popular frozen pizza brand, regularly adds new pizza types and flavours to its existing product mix. Most new pizza products begin selling well immediately with very little promotion or communication about the product. In terms of a product life cycle, the lack of promotion is similar to a _____ product.
questions.explanation: A low-learning product has a short introductory stage because its benefits are self-evident and very little learning is required, so sales start right away with little promotion. High-learning is the opposite: an extended introduction because consumers must be educated.

questions.stem: Which description fits a low-learning product?
options: Significant consumer education is required, so the introduction is extended
Benefits are self-evident, little learning is required, and sales begin immediately
Popularity rises, declines and reappears over the years
Sales rise rapidly and then fall just as rapidly
questions.explanation: A low-learning product's benefits are obvious, so its introduction is short and sales start immediately. An extended introduction with heavy education describes a high-learning product, while cyclical returns and a rapid rise-and-fall describe fashions and fads.

questions.stem: Why is strong distribution especially important for a low-learning product?
options: It is easily copied, so the firm must reach many buyers quickly before imitators do
Consumers need personal selling to understand how to use it
Its sales return in cycles, so stores must restock it every few years
Test marketing is required before it can be sold nationally
questions.explanation: Because a low-learning product is simple to understand, it is also simple for competitors to copy, so the firm needs broad distribution fast to capture sales first. Personal selling to explain usage fits radical or high-learning products, not low-learning ones.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly contrasts low-learning and high-learning products?
options: Low-learning: an extended introduction; high-learning: a short introduction
Low-learning: a rapid rise and fall; high-learning: cyclical returns
