Low: short introduction, immediate sales; high: extended introduction, heavy education
Low-learning: a radical innovation; high-learning: a minor innovation
questions.explanation: Low-learning products sell immediately because their benefits are self-evident; high-learning products need an extended introduction to educate consumers. The option giving low-learning the extended introduction reverses them, and the others confuse PLC shapes with fads, fashions and degrees of innovation.

questions.stem: Pantry Pals is launching a new cookie flavour under its well-established brand. Which PLC pattern and priority should it plan for?
options: A short introduction with immediate sales, so secure strong distribution quickly
A long introduction, so invest in personal selling to educate consumers
A cyclical pattern, so plan to relaunch the flavour in ten years
A slow start, so delay distribution until awareness builds
questions.explanation: A new flavour under a known brand is a low-learning product: buyers understand it instantly, so sales start right away, and because it is easy to copy, strong distribution matters. A long, education-heavy introduction would describe a high-learning product.

questions.stem: In 2017, fidget spinners went from unknown to sold in nearly every corner store within months, then almost vanished a year later. In PLC terms, fidget spinners were a:
questions.explanation: A fad has a rapid rise and an equally rapid fall, giving it a very short life, exactly the fidget-spinner pattern. A fashion product would come back into style in later years, which fidget spinners did not.

questions.stem: Wide-leg jeans were popular in the 1970s, faded, returned in the late 1990s, faded again, and are popular once more. This PLC pattern describes a:
questions.explanation: A fashion product is a style that becomes popular, declines and then returns in cycles over the years. A fad rises and falls quickly and does not keep coming back.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a fashion product from a fad?
options: A fashion rises and falls rapidly; a fad keeps returning in cycles over the years
A fashion requires heavy consumer education; a fad requires almost none
A fashion is a radical innovation; a fad is usually just a minor innovation
A fashion returns in cycles over the years; a fad rises and falls fast with a very short life
questions.explanation: Fashions are cyclical (they return), while fads are brief (fast up, fast down). The option saying a fashion rises and falls rapidly swaps the two definitions, and the others confuse PLC shapes with learning or innovation categories.

questions.stem: A product with a rapid rise and an equally rapid fall in sales, giving it a very short life cycle, is called a(n) _____.
questions.explanation: That is a fad. A fashion also loses popularity, but it returns in cycles over the years instead of disappearing after one quick spike.

questions.stem: Blitz Toys expects its viral plush toy to be a fad. Which plan best fits that PLC shape?
options: Invest in a long consumer-education campaign before sales take off
Plan to relaunch the toy every decade when the style returns
Produce cautiously and sell fast, avoiding big long-term inventory commitments
Harvest the toy for several years to milk a loyal customer base
questions.explanation: A fad's sales rise and fall rapidly, so the firm should move fast and avoid being stuck with stock when demand collapses. Planning periodic relaunches fits a fashion product, and a long education campaign fits a high-learning product.

questions.stem: Which list correctly names the four PLC extension strategies?
options: Market penetration, market development, product development, diversification
Modifying the product, modifying the market, repositioning the product, introducing a new product
Product improvement, line extension, trading up, trading down
questions.explanation: The four ways to extend a PLC are modifying the product, modifying the market, repositioning the product and introducing a new product. Market penetration, market development, product development and diversification form the strategic approaches to growth (Ansoff) matrix, and product improvement, line extension, trading up and trading down are sub-tactics, not the four strategies.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four strategies for extending a product's life cycle?
questions.explanation: Harvesting is a decline-stage strategy that accepts falling sales and cuts support; it does not extend the PLC. Modifying the market, repositioning and introducing a new product are three of the four extension strategies (modifying the product is the fourth).

questions.stem: Brisk Bottling's mature iced-tea brand (1) adds a peach flavour, (2) promotes the tea to seniors, a group that never bought it, and (3) upgrades its ingredients and raises its price to position it as premium. Which extension strategies are these, in order?
options: Modifying the product; modifying the market; repositioning
Modifying the market; modifying the product; repositioning
Repositioning; modifying the market; introducing a new product
Modifying the product; repositioning; modifying the market
questions.explanation: Adding a flavour is a line extension (modifying the product); reaching seniors is finding new customers (modifying the market); upgrading and raising the price is trading up (repositioning). Mixing up the flavour move (product) and the seniors move (market) is the most common error.

questions.stem: Why do marketers use PLC extension strategies?
options: To reduce the array of new-product ideas to a manageable list
To test a product in a limited area before launch
To create primary demand for a brand-new product class
To keep a product from sliding into decline by finding new sources of sales
questions.explanation: Extension strategies stretch a product's life, usually in maturity, by changing the product, the market or the positioning, or by replacing it with a new product. Narrowing ideas and test marketing are NPD-process steps, not life-cycle extension.

questions.stem: As sales of its fifth-generation tablet flatten, TechNorth launches a sixth-generation model designed to replace it and carry its customers forward. Which PLC extension strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Replacing an ageing product with a new one is the fourth extension strategy, introducing a new product. Harvesting is tempting because the old model is fading, but harvesting keeps the old product with reduced support instead of replacing it.

questions.stem: Altering a product's characteristics, such as its quality, performance or appearance, to increase sales is called:
questions.explanation: Changing the product itself (quality, performance, appearance) is product modification, which includes product improvements and line extensions. Market modification leaves the product unchanged and changes who uses it or how it's used.

questions.stem: ClearView, a Canadian window-cleaner brand, reformulates its existing spray so it no longer streaks in freezing temperatures and relaunches it as 'new and improved'. This PLC extension tactic is:
questions.explanation: Upgrading the performance of the existing item is a product improvement, one form of product modification. It is not a line extension, because no new item was added to the line; the same spray was made better.

questions.stem: Glacier Gum (a) reformulates its mint gum so the flavour lasts longer and (b) adds a new watermelon flavour to the line. Which is correct?
options: (a) product improvement; (b) line extension; both are product modifications
(a) is a line extension and (b) is a product improvement
(a) is a market modification and (b) is a product modification
Both are brand extensions, because the brand name stays the same
questions.explanation: Improving an existing item is a product improvement; adding a new flavour to the line is a line extension. Both change the product, so both are product modifications. A brand extension would take the Glacier name into a new product class, which neither move does.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a form of product modification?
options: Adding a new size to an existing line
Promoting an existing product to a new age group
questions.explanation: Promoting the same product to a new age group is finding new customers, a market modification. Improving performance, changing appearance and adding a new size (a line extension) all modify the product.

questions.stem: Sales of Prairie Peak's mature ski wax are slipping because competitors' waxes perform better in very cold snow. Which PLC extension option directly addresses this problem?
options: Creating a new use situation for the existing wax
Harvesting the wax to reap its remaining profit
Test marketing the existing wax in two cities
A product improvement that boosts cold-snow performance
questions.explanation: The problem is the product's performance, so a product improvement (product modification) fixes it directly. Creating a new use situation would change how the wax is used without closing the performance gap, and harvesting gives up on growth.

questions.stem: Kellogg's added two new products to its already broad and well-established brands of breakfast cereals. Because Kellogg's was widely recognized and known for high quality, these products required little or no learning by the customers and achieved sales exceeding 3 million units in the first quarter of their availability. Adding these new products to the range of existing ones is known as:
questions.explanation: A line extension is the addition of a new item to an already existing product line, here two new cereals under well-known Kellogg's brands. Harvesting is the opposite move (cutting support for a declining product), and test marketing is a limited trial, not adding items to a line.

questions.stem: The addition of a new item, such as a flavour, size or variety, to an already existing product line is a(n) _____.
questions.explanation: That is a line extension. A brand extension is different: it moves an existing brand name into a NEW product class (Chapter 7) rather than adding an item within the same line.

questions.stem: Which scenario is a line extension rather than a brand extension?
options: A cereal brand launches a line of frozen pizzas under its name
A running-shoe brand launches branded energy drinks
Banff Tea Co. adds a chai variety to its bagged-tea line
A toothpaste brand launches branded razors
questions.explanation: Adding a new variety within the same product line (bagged tea) is a line extension. The other three take an existing brand name into a new product class, which is a brand extension.

questions.stem: Why do line extensions launched under a well-known brand often sell quickly?
options: Consumers already know and trust the brand, so little learning is required
Line extensions are radical innovations that create primary demand
Line extensions skip the introduction stage because they are test marketed
Line extensions are priced using a harvesting strategy
questions.explanation: A trusted brand name carries over to the new item, so buyers understand and accept it immediately, as with Kellogg's new cereals. Line extensions are typically minor, low-learning additions, not radical innovations.

questions.stem: Nordik Granola's best-selling granola is in maturity. Its manager wants a fast, relatively low-risk way to refresh the brand on the shelf while using the trust the brand has already earned. Which tactic fits best?
options: Diversify into a new product for a new market
Delete the granola from the line
Run a controlled test market of the existing granola
Add new flavours to the existing line
questions.explanation: A line extension (new flavours in the existing line) is a classic maturity tactic that uses brand trust to refresh the line. Diversification is the riskiest growth path, and deletion abandons the product rather than refreshing it.

questions.stem: The slide asking 'Why all the varieties? Good idea?' about Tide's many line extensions suggests that adding too many varieties can backfire by confusing consumers and cannibalizing the brand's existing items.
questions.explanation: True. Line extensions keep a mature brand fresh, but too many varieties can confuse shoppers and pull sales from the brand's own existing items (cannibalization) rather than from competitors.

questions.stem: When a firm's new product takes sales away from the firm's own existing products, this is called:
questions.explanation: Cannibalization means the new product 'eats' the firm's own sales. Market penetration is tempting, but it refers to growing a current product's sales among current customers, often at competitors' expense.

questions.stem: After Lakeshore Dairy launched a premium lactose-free milk, its overall milk sales barely changed: most buyers had simply switched from Lakeshore's regular lactose-free milk. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Sales shifted from Lakeshore's existing product to its own new product, which is cannibalization. It is not the decline stage, because the drop was caused by the firm's own launch, not by outside technology or environmental change.

questions.stem: Sales of Oakridge's original sports drink fell 15% last year. Which explanation indicates cannibalization rather than the decline stage?
options: Consumers switched to a new rival technology
Oakridge cut advertising to harvest the product
Customers switched to Oakridge's own new zero-sugar version
questions.explanation: Cannibalization is when the firm's OWN new product takes sales from its existing product. A shrinking category or a rival technology points to decline, and cutting advertising describes harvesting.

questions.stem: Why is cannibalization a particular concern when a brand adds many line extensions?
options: New items in the line mostly draw buyers from the brand's existing items, not from rivals
Line extensions require radical new learning and consumption patterns by consumers
Line extensions always shrink the brand's distribution and shelf space
Line extensions automatically move the brand into a brand-new market
questions.explanation: Because line extensions are close substitutes for the brand's existing items, many buyers simply switch within the brand, so total sales grow little. Line extensions are typically low-learning additions, not radical innovations.

questions.stem: Which outcome would NOT be described as cannibalization?
options: A competitor's new cereal takes sales from a firm's cereal
A new flavour of a firm's yogurt pulls buyers from its original flavour
A firm's new tablet reduces sales of its own laptops
A firm's new mini size reduces sales of its regular size
questions.explanation: Cannibalization only happens when a firm's own new product takes its own sales. Losing sales to a competitor's product is ordinary competition, not cannibalization.

questions.stem: Suzanne's Soup Company noticed that people only ate soup for lunch, so they added recipes to the back of the labels to encourage people to use their soups to make dinner too. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Creating a new use situation means finding a new occasion or use for an existing product, here dinner instead of only lunch. Product improvements is wrong because the soup itself did not change; only the occasion being promoted did.

questions.stem: Petal & Pine, maker of a gentle baby shampoo, launches ads suggesting that adults with sensitive scalps use the same shampoo. This market modification is:
questions.explanation: The product and its use (washing hair) are unchanged; the firm is targeting a new group of buyers, adults, so this is finding new customers. It is not a new use situation, because the shampoo is still used for the same purpose.

questions.stem: Polar Fizz, a sparkling-water brand, runs a campaign encouraging its current drinkers to have three cans a day instead of one. This market modification is:
questions.explanation: Getting existing customers to use the product more often or in larger amounts is increasing a product's use. It is not a new use situation, because the drink is used the same way, just more frequently.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a market modification with its example?
options: New use situation: promoting baking soda as a fridge deodorizer
Increasing use: marketing a women's razor to men
Finding new customers: label recipes encouraging soup at dinner
New use situation: asking current users to apply sunscreen twice as often
questions.explanation: Baking soda used to deodorize a fridge is a new purpose, so it is a new use situation. A razor marketed to men is finding new customers, soup recipes for dinner are a new use situation, and applying sunscreen more often is increasing use.

questions.stem: Market modification extends a product's life cycle by:
options: improving the product's quality or adding line extensions to it
trading the product up or down to change the value it offers
finding new customers, increasing a product's use, or creating new use situations
deleting the product or harvesting it to reap remaining profits
questions.explanation: Market modification changes the market, not the product: new customers, more use, or new use situations. Improving the product or adding line extensions is product modification.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a market modification?
options: Adding a new flavour to the line
questions.explanation: Adding a new flavour is a line extension, which is a product modification. The other three change who uses the product or how it is used, so they are market modifications.

questions.stem: Hearth Oats' rolled oats are bought almost only for breakfast porridge. Management wants growth without changing the product or targeting a new group of customers. Which tactic fits?
options: Launch a gluten-free oat line (a line extension)
Promote oats as an ingredient in baking and smoothies (a new use situation)
Target university students who don't buy oats (finding new customers)
Upgrade quality and raise the price (trading up)
questions.explanation: Promoting oats for baking and smoothies gives current customers a new occasion to use the unchanged product, which is creating a new use situation. Targeting students would be finding new customers, which management ruled out, and a gluten-free line changes the product.

questions.stem: According to the slides, a firm repositions a product in order to:
options: reduce a large list of new-product ideas to a manageable number
meet changing consumer needs, react to competition, or improve value
test the marketing mix on a limited scale in a defined area
reap minor profits while cutting the product's marketing support
questions.explanation: The slides list three reasons to reposition: meet changing consumer needs, react to competition, or improve value. Reaping minor profits while cutting support is harvesting, a decline strategy rather than an extension strategy.

questions.stem: Fernwood Candles upgrades its existing basic candles with hand-poured soy wax, designer jars and essential oils, and raises their price by 60%. This is:
questions.explanation: Adding value and features to the existing product and raising its price is trading up, a repositioning tactic. It is not a line extension, because Fernwood upgraded its existing candles rather than adding a separate new item to the line.

questions.stem: Without changing the price, Crispo Chips reduces its bag from 235 g to 200 g. In PLC repositioning terms, this is:
questions.explanation: Trading down includes reducing features, quality or price, and also downsizing package contents while keeping the price the same. It is not a product improvement, because consumers get less product rather than a better one.

questions.stem: What is the difference between trading up and trading down?
options: Trading up lowers the price to gain volume; trading down raises the price to signal quality
Trading up targets new customers; trading down targets the firm's current customers
Up adds value or features and raises price; down cuts features, quality, price or package size
Trading up is a market modification; trading down is a product modification
questions.explanation: Trading up = more value for a higher price; trading down = less (fewer features, lower quality, a lower price, or smaller contents at the same price). Both are repositioning moves, not market or product modifications.

questions.stem: Hinterland Outfitters repositions its rugged work boots as stylish urban footwear after noticing young city shoppers adopting the look. Which reason for repositioning does this best illustrate?
options: Catching a rising trend to meet changing consumer needs
Reducing cannibalization of its line extensions
Preparing the boots for test marketing
questions.explanation: Firms reposition to meet changing consumer needs, react to competition or improve value, which includes catching a rising trend like urban workwear. Skimming is an introduction-stage pricing strategy and has nothing to do with repositioning an established product.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of repositioning?
options: A budget hotel chain upgrades its rooms and raises its rates
A cereal maker shrinks box contents but keeps the same price
A juice brand moves from a kids' image to an adult health image
A juice brand adds a new mango flavour to its line
questions.explanation: Adding a new flavour to the line is a line extension (product modification). Upgrading with higher rates is trading up, shrinking contents at the same price is trading down, and moving from a kids' to an adult image changes the product's position, so all three are repositioning.

questions.stem: Dr. Oetker, a popular frozen pizza brand, regularly adds new pizza types and flavours to its existing product mix. In terms of new product innovation, launching new pizza flavours is a/an:
questions.explanation: Minor innovations are small product modifications that require no adjustment or new learning by consumers; nobody needs to be taught how to eat a new pizza flavour. 'Continuous improvement' sounds like the real term, but even a true continuous innovation would change the consumer's routine, which a new flavour does not.

questions.stem: An innovation that changes the consumer's normal routine but does not require totally new learning is a:
questions.explanation: That is a continuous innovation, such as the Swiffer WetJet. A radical innovation goes further and requires new learning and new consumption patterns.

questions.stem: Driverless delivery pods will require Canadians to learn new ways of receiving packages and to adopt entirely new consumption patterns. In terms of degree of innovation, the pods are a:
questions.explanation: Requiring new learning and new consumption patterns is the definition of a radical innovation, like self-driving cars in Figure 8-5. A continuous innovation changes routines but does not demand totally new learning.

questions.stem: Lumio is launching a home 3D food printer, a radical innovation. According to Figure 8-5, its marketing emphasis should be to:
options: gain consumer awareness and achieve wide distribution in many stores
advertise its points of difference and benefits versus competitors
educate consumers via advertising, product trial, personal selling and PR
use very low prices and keep promotion to a minimum, if any
questions.explanation: Radical innovations need consumer education through advertising, product trial and personal selling, and public relations can play a major role. Gaining awareness and wide distribution is the emphasis for minor innovations, which require no learning.

questions.stem: SparkleBright is launching a new and improved version of its toothpaste. Per Figure 8-5, what should its marketing emphasize?
options: Gaining consumer awareness and wide distribution
Educating consumers through personal selling and product trial
Public relations to explain new consumption patterns
Advertising that teaches consumers a new daily routine
questions.explanation: New and improved toothpaste is a minor innovation requiring no new learning, so the emphasis is awareness and wide distribution. Personal selling, product trial and PR-led education are for radical innovations.

questions.stem: Which pairing of innovation type and marketing emphasis is correct?
options: Minor innovation: educate consumers through personal selling
Radical innovation: gain consumer awareness and wide distribution
Continuous innovation: use public relations to teach entirely new consumption patterns
Continuous innovation: advertise points of difference and benefits to consumers
questions.explanation: Figure 8-5 pairs continuous innovation with advertising points of difference and benefits. The other options scramble the table: personal selling and PR-led education belong to radical innovation, and awareness plus wide distribution belongs to minor innovation.

questions.stem: Which example is NOT listed as a radical innovation in Figure 8-5?
questions.explanation: The Swiffer WetJet is Figure 8-5's example of a continuous innovation: it changes the cleaning routine without requiring totally new learning. Self-driving cars, 3D printers and smart speakers require new learning and consumption patterns, so they are radical.

questions.stem: From the consumer's point of view, how new a product is depends on the degree of learning required to use it.
questions.explanation: True. Newness can be judged from the company's view (new to the firm), the market's view (new to the market) or the consumer's view, where it depends on how much learning is required. That consumer view drives the minor, continuous and radical categories.

questions.stem: PulseBand's new wrist tracker has users checking sleep and step data each morning and charging the band nightly. It changes their routine, but anyone who has used a phone app can figure it out. In terms of degree of innovation, this is a:
questions.explanation: Wearable technology is Figure 8-5's example of a continuous innovation: it changes the consumer's normal routine without requiring totally new learning. It is more than minor (which requires no change at all) but less than radical (which requires new consumption patterns).

questions.stem: What percentage of all adopters are early adopters on the adoption curve?
questions.explanation: Early adopters are 13.5% of adopters. 16% is the tempting distractor: it is the share of laggards, and also the combined total of innovators (2.5%) plus early adopters (13.5%).

questions.stem: Priya, a popular Edmonton fitness instructor with slightly above-average education, buys the new FormFit smart mirror soon after launch, and many of her followers buy one after seeing her post about it. Priya is best described as:
options: a member of the early majority
questions.explanation: Early adopters are leaders in social settings with slightly above-average education, and their adoption influences others. Innovators are the venturesome first 2.5% who use multiple information sources; this scenario stresses Priya's social influence, not risk-taking.

questions.stem: Gerald finally buys a smartphone in 2026, long after most Canadians, and only after his neighbours and friends convinced him. He avoids buying on credit because he fears debt. Gerald is a:
questions.explanation: Laggards (16%) fear debt and rely on neighbours and friends as information sources. The late majority is skeptical with below-average social status, but the fear of debt and reliance on neighbours point to laggards.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes innovators from early adopters?
options: Innovators are leaders in social settings; early adopters are venturesome risk-takers
Innovators are 13.5% of adopters; early adopters are 2.5%
Innovators are skeptical; early adopters are deliberate
Innovators are venturesome and use multiple information sources; early adopters are leaders in social settings
questions.explanation: Innovators (2.5%) are venturesome, higher educated and use multiple information sources; early adopters (13.5%) are the leaders in social settings. Calling innovators the social leaders swaps the descriptors, which is the most common trap.

questions.stem: What cumulative percentage of the market has adopted a new product once the early majority has finished adopting?
questions.explanation: Innovators 2.5% + early adopters 13.5% + early majority 34% = 50%. 84% would be the total after the late majority also adopts (50% + 34%).

questions.stem: Which pairing of adopter category and descriptor is NOT correct?
options: Early majority: deliberate; many informal social contacts
Innovators: fear of debt; neighbours and friends are information sources
Late majority: skeptical; below average social status
Early adopters: leaders in social settings
questions.explanation: Fear of debt and relying on neighbours and friends describe laggards, not innovators. Innovators are venturesome, higher educated and use multiple information sources.

questions.stem: On the adoption curve, which adopter category immediately follows the early majority?
questions.explanation: The order is innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards. The late majority (34%, skeptical) follows the early majority (34%, deliberate); laggards come last.

questions.stem: Why do marketers of a new product often focus on winning over early adopters to drive mass adoption?
options: Early adopters make up the largest single group, at 34%
Early adopters are leaders in social settings whose adoption influences the larger majority
Early adopters fear debt, so they respond best to discounts
Early adopters are the most venturesome and use the most information sources
questions.explanation: Early adopters are the leaders in social settings, so their approval influences the deliberate early majority that follows. 'Most venturesome' describes innovators, and 34% describes each of the two majority groups.

questions.stem: The _____, who make up 34% of adopters, are described as skeptical and of below-average social status.
questions.explanation: The late majority is skeptical and has below-average social status. The early majority is also 34%, but it is described as deliberate, with many informal social contacts.

questions.stem: Which list correctly names the four barriers that can deter consumers from adopting a new product?
questions.explanation: The four barriers are usage, value, risk and psychological. Price, place, promotion and product are the 4 Ps, and price, distribution and timing are not on the course's list of adoption barriers.

questions.stem: Many Calgary drivers like the idea of an electric pickup truck but worry it could leave them stranded on a highway at -30 degrees and cost a fortune if the battery fails. Which barrier to adoption is at work?
questions.explanation: Fear of physical danger (being stranded) and economic loss (a costly battery failure) is a risk barrier. It is not a usage barrier, because drivers aren't saying the truck clashes with how they drive; they fear what could go wrong.

questions.stem: A new meal-replacement shake is affordable and as nutritious as a regular lunch, but many Canadians resist it because drinking lunch from a bottle feels at odds with cultural values around shared meals and makes them look like they don't eat properly. Which barrier is this?
questions.explanation: Resistance rooted in cultural differences and image concerns is a psychological barrier. It is not a value barrier: the shake is affordable and nutritious, so the issue isn't a lack of incentive but how it fits people's culture and self-image.

questions.stem: Office workers agree that a new stand-up desk works well and fits easily into their workday, but they see no real advantage over their current desks, so they don't bother switching. Which barrier is this, rather than a usage barrier?
options: Usage barrier: the product is incompatible with existing habits
Value barrier: the product offers no incentive to change
Risk barrier: buyers fear physical harm
Psychological barrier: buyers worry about their image
questions.explanation: When a product works and fits in but offers no incentive to switch, it faces a value barrier. A usage barrier would mean the desk clashes with existing habits, which the scenario rules out.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the four barriers to adoption listed in the course?
questions.explanation: The four barriers are usage, value, risk and psychological. Distribution matters for a launch's success, but it is not one of the listed adoption barriers; risk is the missing fourth barrier.

questions.stem: GlowBrew launched a coffee pod that customers said tasted 'just like every other pod', and it was pulled within a year. According to Figure 8-7, the main issue was:
questions.explanation: A product that isn't meaningfully different from competitors fails because of an insignificant point of difference; the fix is a distinctive, meaningful POD found through consumer research and competitor monitoring. Bad timing would mean the product was fine but launched when consumers weren't eager to buy.

questions.stem: Kinetic Kayaks' new folding kayak flopped: it reached only a few stores, its brand name was hard to remember, and its package didn't show what was inside. Which Figure 8-7 issue and solution apply?
options: Bad timing: launch when consumers are eager to purchase
Insufficient market attractiveness: find a larger target market with growth potential
Poor execution of the marketing mix: align the 4 Ps (incl. name and package) and gain distribution
Insignificant point of difference: research consumers and monitor competitors
questions.explanation: Weak distribution, a poor brand name and an unclear package are marketing-mix execution failures, fixed by aligning the 4 Ps and securing sufficient distribution. Nothing suggests the market itself was too small, so insufficient market attractiveness doesn't fit.

questions.stem: Aurora Pools launched a premium backyard pool line in Yellowknife, but too few households there had the need, space or climate for it, and the market showed no growth. Which failure issue does this illustrate?
options: Poor execution of the marketing mix
questions.explanation: When the target market lacks the need, size or growth potential, the issue is insufficient market attractiveness; the fix is to identify a target market with a need that is large enough and growing. Bad timing concerns when the product launched, not whether the market was big enough.

questions.stem: A product fails because its team never clearly defined its features, benefits and positioning. How does this differ from an 'insignificant point of difference' failure?
options: Incomplete definition: features, benefits and positioning never set; insignificant POD: not meaningfully different
They are the same failure issue, simply described under two different names in the text
Incomplete concept definition is solved by finding a larger market; insignificant POD by better timing
Incomplete concept definition only affects services; insignificant POD only affects goods
questions.explanation: Incomplete new concept definition is fixed by identifying consumer insights, clearly defining features and benefits, and developing a clear positioning. An insignificant POD is fixed by finding a distinctive, meaningful point of difference; they are separate rows in Figure 8-7.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed in the course as a challenge of new product development?
options: Expensive product write-offs if the product fails
Lack of future credibility in the market
Too few sources of new-product ideas
questions.explanation: The listed challenges are an expensive undertaking, high risk of failure, high research costs, extensive time and effort on prototypes and marketing materials, expensive write-offs, and lost credibility. A shortage of ideas is not listed; idea generation draws on many sources.

questions.stem: Why does the course call new products 'the lifeblood of a company' despite their high risk of failure?
options: They guarantee higher profits than the company's mature products
They keep the company's products relevant and bring future revenues into the company
They eliminate the need for any PLC extension strategies later on
They are cheaper to develop than marketing the company's existing products
questions.explanation: The slide quote says new products help make products relevant and bring future revenues into the company. They don't guarantee profits or come cheaply: NPD is expensive and carries a high risk of failure.

questions.stem: Well-established as a Canadian brand, Yummy Brand has identified similar market size, makeup and needs in Costa Rica. Taking its existing product line and updating it to align with the cultural preference in Costa Rica, Yummy introduces its product to several large cities in Costa Rica. The growth strategy followed by Yummy is:
questions.explanation: Market development introduces an existing product to a new market or target audience; adapting the existing line to local culture doesn't make it a new product. Diversification is the trap, but it requires BOTH a new product and a new market.

questions.stem: In the strategic approaches to growth matrix, reaching current customers with a new product is called:
questions.explanation: New product + current market = product development. Market development is the mirror image: a current product taken to new customers.

questions.stem: Rocky Ridge Coffee launches a punch card offering a free drink after nine purchases, aiming to get its existing customers to buy its existing drinks more often. Which growth strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Current product + current customers = market penetration: finding ways to make current products appeal more to current customers. No new product or new market is involved, so neither development strategy applies.

questions.stem: Lakehead Outfitters, known for canoes sold to Ontario cottage owners, launches a line of paddleboards and sells them to the same cottage owners through its existing stores. Which growth strategy is this?
questions.explanation: A new product (paddleboards) offered to current customers (cottage owners) is product development. Diversification would also require a new market, but the customers here are the same.

questions.stem: Prairie Credit Union, a Saskatchewan financial co-operative, opens a chain of pet-grooming salons aimed at urban dog owners in Ontario. Which growth strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Pet grooming is a new product for the credit union, and Ontario dog owners are a new market, so this is diversification. Market development would mean taking its existing financial products to the new market.

questions.stem: What distinguishes market development from product development?
options: Market development creates a new product for new customers; product development sells more to current customers
Market development takes a current product to new customers; product development offers a new product to current customers
Market development is used only internationally; product development only domestically
They are the same strategy described from different viewpoints
questions.explanation: The word before 'development' names what is new: market development = new market, current product; product development = new product, current market. Market development is not limited to other countries; a new domestic segment also counts.

questions.stem: Which statement about the strategic approaches to growth is NOT correct?
options: Market penetration means finding ways to make current products appeal to current customers
Market development means reaching new customers with a current product
Diversification means reaching current customers with a new product
Product development means reaching current customers with a new product
questions.explanation: Diversification means reaching NEW customers with a new product; reaching current customers with a new product is product development. The other three statements match Figure 8-8 exactly.

questions.stem: Pemmican Provisions has saturated its home market in Manitoba with its jerky. Management wants to grow without developing any new products. Which strategy should it consider?
options: Market development: sell the same jerky in new markets such as B.C. or the U.S.
Product development: launch new snack bars for Manitoba customers
Diversification: enter a new industry in a new region
Product rationalization: retain only the best sellers
questions.explanation: With the home market saturated and no new products allowed, the remaining growth path is taking the current product to new markets, which is market development. Product development and diversification both require new products, which management ruled out.

questions.stem: Why is diversification usually seen as the riskiest of the four strategic approaches to growth?
options: It relies only on current customers, who may grow tired of the firm's products
Both the product and the market are new to the firm, so it has experience with neither
It requires cutting prices on the firm's current products
It cannot be combined with test marketing or a regional rollout
questions.explanation: Diversification pairs a new product with a new market, so the firm can't lean on existing product know-how or customer knowledge. Relying on current customers describes market penetration or product development, not diversification.

questions.stem: Taking an existing product line into a new country, even after adapting it to local cultural preferences, is still market development rather than diversification.
questions.explanation: True. Adapting an existing line to local tastes doesn't make it a new product, so the move is a current product in a new market: market development. Diversification requires both a new product and a new market.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the first four steps of the NPD process?
options: Idea generation, new product development strategy, business analysis, screening and evaluation
New product development strategy, idea generation, screening and evaluation, business analysis
Idea generation, screening and evaluation, development, business analysis
New product development strategy, screening and evaluation, idea generation, development
questions.explanation: The process starts with strategy, then idea generation, screening and evaluation, and business analysis (followed by development, test marketing and commercialization). Starting with idea generation is a common slip; the firm first sets a strategic focus so it knows what kinds of ideas to look for.

questions.stem: Which step comes immediately before development in the NPD process?
questions.explanation: Business analysis (step 4) comes right before development (step 5): the firm projects features, marketing strategy and finances before paying to build prototypes. Screening and evaluation is step 3, two steps earlier.

questions.stem: Step 6 of the seven-step NPD process is _____.
questions.explanation: Test marketing is step 6, between development (step 5) and commercialization (step 7). Commercialization is the final step, the full launch.

questions.stem: Why does the NPD process screen out weak ideas before business analysis and development?
options: Screening is legally required before a patent can be filed
Development must begin before any financial projections are made
Consumers refuse to test more than one prototype
Later steps are far more expensive, so eliminating poor ideas early saves money
questions.explanation: The process is a funnel: early steps like screening and concept testing are cheap, while prototypes, test markets and launches are costly, so weak ideas are dropped as early as possible. Development does not come before financial projections; business analysis precedes it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven steps of the NPD process?
questions.explanation: Market penetration is a strategic approach to growth (Ansoff matrix), not an NPD step. Screening and evaluation, business analysis and commercialization are steps 3, 4 and 7.

questions.stem: Aspen Audio has narrowed 200 ideas to three promising earbud concepts and is now projecting each concept's costs, profitability and legal issues. Which step is it in, and what comes next?
options: Screening and evaluation; next is business analysis
Business analysis; next is test marketing
questions.explanation: Projecting costs, profitability and legal issues is business analysis (step 4), and development (step 5, building prototypes) comes next. 'Business analysis; next is test marketing' names the right step but skips development; test marketing happens only after prototypes exist.

questions.stem: In the NPD process, business analysis comes after development, once a prototype exists that can be costed out.
questions.explanation: False. Business analysis is step 4 and development is step 5, so the firm makes financial projections BEFORE building prototypes. Corrected statement: business analysis comes before development.

questions.stem: The first step of the NPD process, new product development strategy, aims to:
options: brainstorm as many new-product ideas as possible from many sources
identify a new-product development focus that meets company objectives
make financial projections for each promising concept
create prototypes and test them internally and with consumers
questions.explanation: Step 1 sets the focus: what kinds of new products fit the company's objectives, using company objectives and a SWOT analysis. Brainstorming comes next, in idea generation.

questions.stem: Cascade Cosmetics reviews its corporate objectives and conducts a SWOT analysis of the company and its brands to decide what kinds of new products to pursue. Which NPD step is this?
questions.explanation: Using company objectives and a SWOT analysis to set the new-product focus is the new product development strategy step. Business analysis is tempting because it is also analytical, but it evaluates a specific concept's features, marketing mix and finances.

questions.stem: Tundra Tools takes apart a competitor's new cordless drill to see how it works and collects suggestions from its suppliers and front-line staff. These activities belong to which NPD step?
questions.explanation: Reverse engineering competitors' products and gathering suggestions from suppliers and employees are sources of new ideas, so this is idea generation. Development involves building and testing Tundra's own prototypes, not studying a rival's product.

questions.stem: What distinguishes idea generation from screening and evaluation?
options: Idea generation uses concept tests; screening and evaluation uses brainstorming
Idea generation makes financial projections; screening and evaluation builds prototypes
Idea generation is step 3; screening and evaluation is step 2
Idea generation brainstorms many ideas; screening and evaluation narrows them to a manageable list
questions.explanation: Idea generation (step 2) widens the funnel by brainstorming; screening and evaluation (step 3) narrows it, using internal evaluation and external concept tests. Saying idea generation uses concept tests reverses their tools.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a typical source in the idea generation step?
options: Financial projections from the business analysis step
questions.explanation: Financial projections come later, in business analysis (step 4), and evaluate concepts rather than generate them. Employees, co-workers, consumers, crowdsourcing and competitors are all idea sources.

questions.stem: The stage of a new product development process called _____ attempts to reduce the array of brainstorming ideas down to a manageable list of promising concepts.
questions.explanation: The third stage, screening and evaluation, reduces the array of brainstorming ideas to a manageable list of promising concepts. Idea generation is the step before it, which creates that array of ideas in the first place.

questions.stem: Before building anything, Polaris Pet Co. shows 400 dog owners written descriptions and sketches of five new toy ideas and asks how likely they would be to buy each. This is a:
questions.explanation: Showing consumers descriptions or sketches of an idea (not an actual product) is a concept test, part of screening and evaluation. A prototype test needs a working model, which comes later in development.

questions.stem: How does a concept test differ from the consumer testing done in the development step?
options: Concept tests sell the product in a limited area; development tests use descriptions
Concept tests are internal only; development tests are external only
Concept tests show a description of the idea; development tests let consumers try a prototype
Concept tests make financial projections; development tests check legal issues
questions.explanation: A concept test (screening) presents a description of the idea, while development tests consumers' reactions to a working prototype. Selling in a limited area is test marketing, a later step.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the screening and evaluation step?
options: To eliminate weak ideas, leaving a manageable list of promising concepts
To generate as many new-product ideas as possible from many sources
To set the company's overall new-product focus using a SWOT analysis
To launch the product with full-scale production and marketing support
questions.explanation: Screening and evaluation weeds out weak ideas cheaply, before money goes into business analysis and prototypes. Generating ideas is the previous step, and setting the focus is step 1.

questions.stem: Which activity does NOT belong in the screening and evaluation step?
options: Selling finished units in two test cities
Dropping ideas with weak consumer interest
questions.explanation: Selling finished units in defined cities is test marketing (step 6). Screening and evaluation uses internal technical evaluation and external concept tests to drop weak ideas.

questions.stem: Screening and evaluation is step _____ of the seven-step NPD process.
questions.explanation: Screening and evaluation is step 3, after strategy (1) and idea generation (2) and before business analysis (4). Step 4 is the tempting distractor because both steps evaluate concepts.

questions.stem: Specifying a new product's features and marketing strategy and making financial projections happens in which NPD step?
questions.explanation: Business analysis (step 4) identifies the product's key features and marketing strategy and makes financial projections, including production, legal and profitability issues. Screening and evaluation comes earlier and narrows ideas using concept tests.

questions.stem: Before any prototypes exist, Fjord Foods' team estimates production costs, checks whether its new kelp snack meets food-labelling laws, and projects five-year profits. This is:
questions.explanation: Assessing production, legal and profitability issues on paper is business analysis. Development would involve building and testing the actual snack prototype.

questions.stem: Which comparison of business analysis and development is accurate?
options: Business analysis builds prototypes; development makes financial projections
Business analysis follows development so that the prototype can be costed
Both steps involve selling the product on a limited basis in test areas
Business analysis does the paper projections; development builds and tests prototypes
questions.explanation: Business analysis (step 4) is the paper-and-spreadsheet check; development (step 5) turns the idea into a working prototype and tests it. The 'follows development' option reverses their order.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT assessed during business analysis?
options: Repeat purchase rates in test cities
questions.explanation: Repeat purchase rates in test cities come from test marketing (step 6), long after business analysis. Business analysis assesses production, legal and profitability issues plus the planned features and marketing mix.

questions.stem: Business analysis is done before development so that money isn't spent building prototypes for products that won't be profitable.
questions.explanation: True. Prototypes are expensive, so the firm first checks features, marketing strategy, production, legal and profitability issues. Only concepts that make business sense move on to development.

questions.stem: In the NPD process, the step that turns the idea on paper into a prototype and tests it internally and with consumers is:
questions.explanation: Development (step 5) creates the prototype and tests it internally (company assessments) and externally (consumer tests on prototypes). Business analysis comes just before it and works on paper, not with physical models.

questions.stem: Orca Outdoor builds 30 working models of its new insulated water bottle, drop-tests them in its lab, and gives them to hikers for a month of real use. This is the _____ step.
questions.explanation: Building working models and testing them in the lab and with consumers is the development step. It is not test marketing, because the bottles are lent out for testing, not sold in a defined market area.

questions.stem: A student says: 'Development is when we offer the finished product for sale in a couple of cities.' What is the correct contrast?
options: That is commercialization; development is the concept-testing step
That is test marketing; development creates and tests prototypes
That is business analysis; development is really idea generation
The student is correct; that is exactly what development means
questions.explanation: Selling the finished product on a limited basis in defined areas is test marketing (step 6). Development (step 5) is about creating and testing prototypes; concept tests belong to screening and evaluation.

questions.stem: The word 'development' appears in both the NPD process and the strategic approaches to growth. Which statement is NOT correct?
options: In the NPD process, development means building and testing prototypes
Product development in the growth matrix means reaching current customers with a new product
In the NPD process, development means taking a current product to a new market
Market development in the growth matrix means reaching new customers with a current product
questions.explanation: Taking a current product to a new market is market development, a growth strategy, not the NPD development step. In the NPD process, development means turning the idea into a prototype and testing it.

questions.stem: Which steps come immediately before and immediately after development in the NPD process?
options: Screening and evaluation before; business analysis after
Business analysis before; test marketing after
Idea generation before; screening and evaluation after
questions.explanation: The sequence is business analysis (4), development (5), test marketing (6). Putting business analysis after development is the most common ordering mistake.

questions.stem: Offering a product for sale on a limited basis in a defined area to gauge consumer reactions and test the marketing strategy is:
questions.explanation: That is test marketing (step 6). A regional rollout is tempting, but it is a full launch introduced area by area during commercialization, not a limited trial to gather information.

questions.stem: Bluenose Beverages pays a group of Halifax grocers to stock and display its new energy drink for eight weeks so it can track sales. Which type of test market is this?
questions.explanation: Paying retailers to stock and display the product is a controlled test market. A standard test market sells the product through regular channels in actual cities without paying stores to carry it.

questions.stem: Why might a manufacturer decide to skip test marketing for a new line of washing machines?
options: Washing machines are low-learning products that need no real launch
Test marketing is expensive, alerts competitors, and is impractical for durable goods
Test marketing is only permitted for services, not for physical goods
Washing machines must be commercialized before business analysis is done
questions.explanation: Test marketing is not always necessary: it is costly, it tips off competitors, and it isn't practical for durable goods like appliances. That is why the step is done only 'if necessary'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a type of test market?
questions.explanation: A regional rollout is part of commercialization: a full launch introduced sequentially into geographic areas. Standard, controlled and simulated test markets are the three types of test market.

questions.stem: Before deciding whether to go national, Cedar Snacks sells its new maple popcorn through normal grocery channels in Sudbury and Kamloops for six months and tracks repeat purchases. Which type of test market is this?
questions.explanation: Selling through regular channels in actual cities to gauge reactions is a standard test market. It isn't a regional rollout, because Cedar hasn't committed to a full launch; it is still gathering information to decide.

questions.stem: Shoppers recruited to a research facility watch a set of TV ads, including one for Lumen's new shampoo, then shop in a mock store set up to look like a real drugstore. Which type of test market is this?
questions.explanation: Exposing consumers to ads and then letting them shop in a simulated store is a simulated (laboratory) test market. A concept test would show only a description of the idea, not a finished product on a shelf.

questions.stem: _____ is the step when the new product is brought to market with full-scale production, sales, and marketing support.
questions.explanation: Commercialization is the final NPD step: the product is brought to market with full-scale production, sales and marketing support. Test marketing is the step before it and involves only limited sales in defined areas.

questions.stem: After strong test results, Muskoka Mints ramps up to full production, ships to retailers across Canada and launches a national TV and social media campaign. This is:
questions.explanation: Full-scale production with all areas of the marketing mix implemented nationally is commercialization. Test marketing has already happened; it was the limited trial that produced the 'strong test results'.

questions.stem: Wildrose Kombucha launches in Alberta in March, Saskatchewan and Manitoba in June, and B.C. in September so production and marketing can build up gradually. This approach is:
questions.explanation: Introducing a product sequentially into geographic areas so production and marketing can build is a regional rollout, part of commercialization. It is not a standard test market, because each region receives a full launch rather than a limited trial.

questions.stem: How does a regional rollout differ from test marketing?
options: A regional rollout is a limited trial; test marketing is a full-scale launch
A rollout is a full launch done area by area; a test market is a limited trial before deciding
A regional rollout happens during development; test marketing during business analysis
They are the same thing, simply described in different words
questions.explanation: A regional rollout is a sequenced full-scale launch (commercialization), while test marketing is a limited sale used to gauge consumer reactions and test the marketing strategy. Calling the rollout a limited trial reverses the two.

questions.stem: Once commercialization begins, the new product enters which stage of the product life cycle?
questions.explanation: Commercialization is the full launch, which is where the PLC begins with the introduction stage. 'Development' is an NPD step, not a PLC stage, and it happens before commercialization.
